Jesus, upon His ascension back into His heavenly home, gave a final directive to His disciples, both to those physically present as He disappeared into the clouds, and to the myriad of believers who would come to know Him down through the ages. The story of His life and His gospel were to be preached unto all the world by those who called Him Lord. This global spreading of the Word, would, in the later vision of John, be proclaimed as one of the prerequisites of Jesus’ triumphant return at the end of time. John himself would be seen as a harbinger of these end times, based on Jesus’ words as recorded by John … If I will that he [John] tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. John 21:22.

The early Christians, understandably, felt that the return of Christ was imminent, even within the first century. The rapid expansion of Christianity, the complete moral depravity of the Roman culture, and the increasing intensity of persecution against them seemed to point to a swift and triumphant return of their Lord.

Now, two thousand years since Christ gave that promise, His soon return seems just as imminent as it did to the first century believers. Speculation on the time of His return, the manner of it, and the contributing factors are always current and controversial subjects. In the light of this continued earnest expectation of the end times, what have we to learn about our interpretations of prophecy from those who have attempted to decipher the prophetic portions of Scripture in earlier ages?

Jesus' first coming was surrounded and enveloped by perhaps the most recognizable misinterpretation of prophecy in the Bible. Roughly four hundred years of relative silence from God precluded His entry into the world in a physical, human body. His birth would be unnoticed in a society that was not only in desperate need of, but also expecting, a Savior to arrive. Daniel, writing the words God gave him, had told of a Messiah to come, and had even given a time that He would appear. Now, the Jews seethed under Roman rule, hanging their hopes on what they thought would be a sudden and triumphant extermination of the Roman troops and influence from their lands. To us, it is glaringly obvious that their interpretation of prophecy was not only incorrect, but for many, would lead them astray so that they did not even recognize or acknowledge the true Redeemer that was sent to them.

But what was it that caused this misinterpreted view? To us, it seems completely in order that Jesus would focus on the poor and destitute rather than opposing an occupying army. Jewish historians give an intriguing, but scarcely surprising, answer to the failure of the majority of their people to recognize Christ for who He was.

The religious atmosphere of first century Israel was one defined by corruption, bribery, lust for power, and all the unsavory aspects of a completely politically motivated upper class.

The priests, once chosen by God to be His servants in sanctifying His children, had sunk to buying their positions of service, most notably in the high priest’s office, where God had ordained one high priest to serve the people throughout his life. In Jesus’ day, however, the responsibilities of leading the children of Israel were divvied out, the role often changing hands on one-year terms. Becoming a high priest was a matter of birth. Most high priests came from several large, influential, and wealthy families, as one often had to buy into the opportunity of this office.

It was not only the high priest’s office that was corrupted, but most levels of prominent spiritual leadership were filled by the wealthy elites who had the connections and wealth to be placed into roles of importance amongst the Jews.

This unsavory backdrop gives even more clarity to Jesus’ feelings on the religious leaders of His day. These imposters did not hold their priestly positions to serve His Father, they held them for their own gain, turning the temple into a marketplace and holding the common people hostage through their disputes on the minutiae of the Law.

Unsurprisingly, these leaders looked for a Messiah who would fit their goals, their ideals, and their morals, rather than one that would rebuke and chastise them for their hypocrisy, greed, and selfish ambition. Their view of prophecy had been so twisted and corrupted by their lifestyle that even the miracle of a resurrection could not sway them to view Christ’s power as coming from God. This misconstrued expectation of a conquering commander, riding a horse of war over the political enemies of these elites was pandered to the common Jew as well. Centuries of fighting for just the freedom to worship, as in the case of the Maccabees and the Greeks, had deeply imprinted a sense of nationalism into the collective mind of the Jewish people. The ones who bought into it the most were the ones who received the most from this system of exclusive access to God and His promises. To those who were repressed by the stringent and often man-made laws of Jewish society, a God of peace and love who would draw the needy of the world to Him was more welcome than a Saviour who would simply install another earthly government to rule the poor, oppress the widows, and reward the wicked.

This was not the last time an oppressed people would be deceived, as Roman rule would witness another major misstep in the collective interpretations of God’s people. This time, the teachings of Jesus and the words of His disciples would be misinterpreted to fit the changing political and religious landscape of fourth century Rome. The year was 306, and Diocletian, one of the most brutal persecutors of Christians in the Roman Empire, had abdicated from his position as Caesar. In his wake, he left three contenders for his throne. One of those vying for the seat of power was a young general, experienced in politics, and power hungry. His name was Constantine, son of a prominent Roman officer and a lowly Greek Christian, Helena.

From his youth, Constantine followed in his father’s footsteps, fighting throughout the empire, rising to a rank of general. Now, on campaign in Britain, he turned his eyes to the ultimate prize of a Roman politico, the title of Caesar, and the seat of the emperor.

Constantine’s line to the throne was through his father. Diocletian had, during his rule, appointed additional Caesars to aid in ruling the empire. Constantine’s father was one of these, and despite being simply appointed to the position, it was expected that his status as a Caesar would pass to his son. Matters were not as simple as a mere transfer of titles, however.

Constantine’s rise was bloody, but his grip on power was set, until he remained the sole contender for the throne. The stage was set. He quickly undid the harsh decrees of Diocletian, legalizing Christianity and removing the persecution that had leveled churches, scattered families, and hunted down bishops and other church leadership. Almost overnight, a peace previously unheard of was gifted to these hounded believers.

The changes that Constantine made did not end, however, with merely legalizing Christianity. His sympathies ran deeper, and he made further moves to legitimize it as not only an accepted religion, but as the state religion.

To Christians eager for the return of Christ, this seemed almost unbelievable. In the span of a few short years the government had gone from crucifying, beheading, and torturing them to holding them up as examples to the rest of the empire. The favor seems to have affected the clarity with which they viewed the apparent reconciliation of the world to the church. Not only would they accept a position of power in the empire, but they would also accept Constantine as a benefactor and protector of the church itself. In their minds, the day of the Lord was come, and Constantine was the rod of iron with which God would rule.

And rule he did. The course of the church was soon swayed by this new and outside influence. Constantine sat in on meetings of the bishops, even though at the time he was not baptized nor was he even seeking baptism. The church’s new position as a tool of the state brought schisms, in-fighting, and contention at every turn. There remained a remnant, but most of the church would fall under the sway of a man motivated by a hunger for power, wealth, and influence.

Constantine would be baptized before his death, lending him even further credibility in the eyes of a straying church. Now separated from its original identity as sheep in this world, the coming centuries would see “Christians” become ravening wolves, destroying, killing, and corrupting.

In a matter more recently related to us as Anabaptists, the tale of the infamous Muensterites gives us a further example of the perils of misinterpreting prophecy, especially the prophecy regarding the second coming of Christ.

One of the great disadvantages of a heavily persecuted group is a tendency to lack stability, as evidenced by the varying beliefs developed by Anabaptist groups of the movement's first fifty years. Persecution would deprive a congregation of their leaders, who were often those most targeted by the authorities. A missing elder meant less teaching, which in turn led to more difficulty in guidance, and corrective doctrine. Even the most sincere and interconnected groups could fall into errors developed because of the lack of leadership to bring Biblical clarity and balance the brotherhood.

The situation in the Netherlands was of a rather volatile strain approaching the 1530s. Throughout the country, the Catholic Church remained the predominant religion, clinging to their power through ruthless displays of physical force, most often directed towards the minority Protestant congregations. This focus on quelling the Protestant influence was momentarily successful in this instance, with most of their groups dissolving and reintegrating into the Catholic Church or other groups.

One of the groups that was on the receiving end of this minor diaspora was the fledging Dutch Anabaptist church. For those Protestants who still refused to join the Catholics, the Anabaptists often became their choice of church, rapidly swelling their ranks. This had a profound effect on the local strain of Anabaptism, which without a doubt was fervent, but quite prone to chaos and upheaval.

By 1534 the tensions of this influx of new believers reached a breaking point, and the Anabaptist church of the Netherlands split into two main factions. The first, led by the two Philips brothers, Dirk and Obbe, adhered to the New Testament teachings of separation from church and state, as well as nonresistance. This would be the church of Menno Simmons, and the root of the Mennonite churches of today.

The other faction held to more radical beliefs, led by Jan Matthysz and Jan of Leiden. These two men became increasingly fanatical in their views of Christ’s return, believing that they would be central figures, instrumental in a kingdom that God would set up on Earth.

At the same time, social unrest was brewing, and spilled over in the city of Munster, located in northwest Germany, where the common people rose up, overthrowing their city’s government and expelling their Catholic bishop. The two Jans were quick to act, contacting the new leaders of the city, and eventually winning them over to their views.

The Jans moved to Munser in early 1534, and began sending out prophets and messengers, who called all “Anabaptists” to congregate at this “New Jerusalem”. The unrest of the area made their message all the more appealing, and thousands streamed into the city, intent in being part of this apocalyptic return of Christ.

There was, in fact, an apocalyptic return on the horizon, but not a return of Christ. This one came in the form of the ousted Catholic bishop, who swiftly set siege to the city. His army would stay there for eighteen months.

Inside the city, Jan Matthysz, proclaiming a vision was given to him for a deliverance of the city, left its walls to parade outside, proclaiming a swift delivery of the enemy into his hands. His vision, however, failed him, as he was swiftly delivered into the hands of the enemy, where he was beheaded, and his head set on a pike in front Munster’s gates.

Inside the walls, Jan of Leiden took leadership, ignoring the famine, death, and chaos that now ran rampant within the besieged walls. Instead, he began promoting polygamy, defending it from the Old Testament, killing at least one woman who refused to marry him, and at one point, having sixteen wives.

This abomination soon led to its required end as the city was overcome, with a heavy slaughter being carried out against its inhabitants. The leaders, Jan of Leiden being the most prominent, were captured, tortured, and killed. Their bodies were hung in iron cages on the tower of St. Lamberts Church, the Catholic church in Munster. To this day, the cages still hang, a bleak reminder of the pride and rashness of the two Jans, determined to see their end-time interpretation fulfilled.

In all three of these examples, the prophecy contained in God’s Word was twisted into results that strayed far from the will of God for His children. For the Jews, it caused them to miss the Messiah, failing to recognize the greatest promise God had given them. The fourth century Christians, chafing under the horrific persecution of Diocletian, accepted Constantine as a deliverer, seeing him as a fulfillment of God’s judgement against the kingdoms of this world. Instead of peace, they would sink into a state of ungodliness worse than the pagans around them, with the Catholic Church straying into sin more horrible than even their pagan society. Lastly, the troubled visions and interpretations of the 16th century Munsterites would lead them to an awful fate, sullying the name of the true church.

What have we to learn from these grave errors of those before us? In our time, the end seems imminent, and we are beset with those who would have us believe that we are truly the last of the Christians.

Luke has recorded the instructions of Jesus on this point: …The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see it. And they shall say to you, See here; or, see there: go not after them, nor follow them –Luke 17: 22-23. Here are instructions for our conduct in the last days. Let us not be running after the rumors of the end times but let us be obedient to the final admonition of our Lord—that we spread the Word of God and the Gospel of His Son, Jesus throughout the world … and then shall the end come –Matthew 24:14.

Иисус, возвратившись на небо при Своём восхождении, дал последнее указание Своим ученикам — как тем, кто физически присутствовал, когда Он исчез в облаках, так и множеству верующих, которые будут познавать Его на протяжении веков. Историю Его жизни и Его Евангелие должны были проповедовать всем миру те, кто называет Его Господом. Это вселенское распространение Слова, как позже в видении Иоанна, было провозглашено одним из условий торжественного возвращения Иисуса в конце времён. Сам Иоанн был увиден как предвестник этих последних дней, исходя из слов Иисуса, записанных Иоанном … Если я захочу, чтобы он [Иоанн] остался, пока приду я, — что тебе до того? иди за мною. John 21:22.

Ранние христиане, что естественно, считали возвращение Христа неминуемым, даже в первом веке. Быстрый рост христианства, полная нравственная развращённость римской культуры и усиливающаяся интенсивность гонений против них казались указывать на скорое и торжественное пришествие их Господа.

Теперь, спустя две тысячи лет с тех пор, как Христос дал это обещание, Его скоро возвращение кажется так же непосредственным, как и для верующих первого века. Спекуляции о времени Его возвращения, о его способе и сопутствующих факторах всегда являются актуальными и спорными темами. В свете этого постоянного горячего ожидания конца времён, чему нам следует научиться из толкований пророчеств тех, кто пытался разгадать пророческие места Писания в прежние века?

Первое пришествие Иисуса было окружено и поглощено, возможно, самым узнаваемым неверным толкованием пророчества в Библии. Примерно четырёхсотлетняя относительная тишина от Бога предшествовала Его входу в мир в физическом, человеческом теле. Его рождение осталось бы незаметным в обществе, которое не только крайне нуждалось в Спасителе, но и ожидая Его прихода. Даниил, записывая слова, данные ему Богом, предсказал приход Мессии и даже указал время, когда Он явится. Но евреи кипели недовольством под римским владычеством, возлагая надежды на то, что, по их мнению, должно было быть внезапным и триумфальным изгнанием римских войск и влияния из их земель. Для нас совершенно очевидно, что их толкование пророчества было не только ошибочным, но для многих привело их в заблуждение так, что они не узнали и не признали истинного Искупителя, посланного им.

Но что же вызвало такое искажённое представление? Нам кажется вполне естественным, что Иисус сосредоточился бы на бедных и нищих, а не на противостоянии оккупационной армии. Еврейские историки дают интригующий, но отнюдь не удивительный ответ на неспособность большинства их народа распознать Христа.

Религиозная атмосфера Израиля первого века была определена коррупцией, взяточничеством, жаждой власти и всеми нелицеприятными сторонами полностью политизированного высшего класса.

Священники, некогда избранные Богом быть Его служителями в освящении народа, опустились до покупки своих служений, наиболее заметно — в сан первосвященника, где Бог повелел одному первосвященнику служить народу в течение всей его жизни. Во дни Иисуса обязанности вести народ Израиля, однако, раздавались, и роль часто менялась ежегодно. Стать первосвященником стало делом рождения. Большая часть первосвященников происходила из нескольких крупных, влиятельных и богатых семей, поскольку часто приходилось выкупать возможность занять этот пост.

Коррупцией был заражён не только сан первосвященника; большинство видных духовных руководящих мест занимали состоятельные элиты, имевшие связи и богатство, чтобы быть поставленными на важные позиции среди иудеев.

Этот непривлекательный фон ещё яснее освещает отношение Иисуса к религиозным лидерам Его времени. Эти самозванцы не держали своих священнических должностей, чтобы служить Его Отцу; они занимали их ради собственной выгоды, превращая храм в рынок и держа простых людей в заложниках через споры о мелочах Закона.

Неудивительно, что эти лидеры ожидали Мессию, который соответствовал бы их целям, их идеалам и их морали, а не Того, кто упрекал бы и наказал их за лицемерие, жадность и самолюбивые амбиции. Их представление о пророчестве было настолько исковеркано и развращено образом их жизни, что даже чудо воскресения не могло склонить их к признаю силы Христа как исходящей от Бога. Это искажённое ожидание завоевателя-командующего, въезжающего на боевом коне и раздавливающего политических врагов этих элит, находило отклик и у простых иудеев. Века борьбы за свободу поклонения, как в случае с Маккавеями и греками, глубоко отпечатали националистическое чувство в коллективном сознании еврейского народа. Те, кто в большей степени покупались на это, получали наибольшую выгоду от системы исключительного доступа к Богу и Его обещаниям. Для угнетённых строгими и часто человеческими законами еврейского общества Бог мира и любви, который притягивает нуждающихся мира к Себе, был желаннее, чем Спаситель, который просто установил бы ещё одно земное правление, чтобы править бедными, угнетать вдов и вознаграждать нечестивых.

Это не было последним случаем, когда угнетённый народ оказался обманут — римское владычество станет свидетелем ещё одной крупной ошибки в коллективных толкованиях Божьего народа. На этот раз учения Иисуса и слова Его учеников были неправильно истолкованы, чтобы соответствовать меняющемуся политическому и религиозному ландшафту Рима IV века. Был 306 год, и Диоклетиан, один из самых жестоких гонителей христиан в Римской империи, отрёкся от своего поста кесаря. После него осталось три претендента на трон. Одним из тех, кто претендовал на власть, был молодой генерал, опытный в политике и жаждущий власти. Его звали Константин, сын видного римского офицера и простой гречанки-христианки Елены.

С молодых лет Константин шёл по стопам отца, сражаясь по всей империи и поднимаясь до звания генерала. Теперь, находясь в кампании в Британии, он обратил взгляд на высшую награду римского политика — титул кесаря и трон императора.

Линия Константина к трону пролегала через его отца. Диоклетиан во время своего правления назначил дополнительных кесарей для помощи в управлении империей. Отец Константина был одним из них, и, несмотря на то что он был просто назначен на должность, ожидалось, что его статус кесаря перейдёт к его сыну. Однако всё оказалось не так просто, как простая передача титулов.

Подъём Константина был кровавым, но его хватка власти устояла, и вскоре он остался единственным претендентом на трон. Сцена была готова. Он быстро отменил жёсткие указы Диоклетиана, легализовав христианство и прекратив преследования, которые разрушали церкви, рассекали семьи и выслеживали епископов и иных церковных лидеров. Почти за одну ночь этим притеснённым верующим была дарована невиданная прежде тишина и покой.

Но изменения, внесённые Константином, не ограничивались лишь легализацией христианства. Его симпатии шли глубже, и он предпринял дальнейшие шаги, чтобы узаконить его не только как признанную религию, но и как государственную религию.

Для христиан, жаждущих возвращения Христа, это казалось почти невероятным. В течение всего нескольких лет власть перешла от распинания, обезглавливания и пыток к возвеличиванию их в пример остальной империи. Это благоволение, по-видимому, повлияло на ясность их восприятия видимого примирения мира с церковью. Они не только приняли бы положение власти в империи, но и признали бы Константина благодетелем и защитником самой церкви. В их умах настал день Господень, и Константин был железным жезлом, которым Бог будет управлять.

И он действительно правил. Курс церкви вскоре был подвержен этому новому внешнему влиянию. Константин присутствовал на собраниях епископов, хотя в то время он ещё не был крещён и даже не стремился к крещению. Новое положение церкви как инструмента государства привело к расколам, внутренним конфликтам и спорам на каждом шагу. Остаток верных оставался, но большая часть церкви попала под власть человека, движимого голодом к власти, богатству и влиянию.

Константин принял крещение перед смертью, что ещё больше укрепило его авторитет в глазах заблудшей церкви. Отделившись от своей первоначальной идентичности как овец в этом мире, в последующие столетия «христиане» превращались в хищных волков, уничтожающих, убивающих и развращающих.

В более недавнем для нас примере, связанном с анабаптистами, история печально известных менстеритов даёт ещё один пример опасностей неверного толкования пророчеств, особенно пророчеств о втором пришествии Христа.

Одним из больших недостатков сильно преследуемой группы является склонность к нестабильности, о чём свидетельствуют различные верования, развившиеся у анабаптистских групп в первые пятьдесят лет движения. Гонения лишали общину её руководителей, которые часто становились наиболее уязвимыми для властей. Отсутствие старейшины означало меньше учения, что влекло за собой трудности в руководстве и исправлении учения. Даже самые искренние и взаимосвязанные группы могли впасть в ошибки, возникшие из-за отсутствия руководства, которое могло бы принести библейскую ясность и уравновесить братство.

Ситуация в Нидерландах к 1530-м годам была довольно нестабильной. По всей стране католическая церковь оставалась доминирующей религией, удерживая власть посредством беспощадных проявлений физической силы, направленных чаще всего против меньшинственных протестантских общин. Эта цель по усмирению протестантского влияния временно оказалась успешной, поскольку большинство таких групп распалось и реинтегрировалось в католическую церковь или в другие объединения.

Одной из групп, оказавшихся на приёме этого небольшого рассеяния, была зарождающаяся голландская анабаптистская церковь. Для тех протестантов, кто всё ещё отказывался присоединиться к католикам, анабаптисты часто становились выбором, и их ряды быстро росли. Это оказало глубокое влияние на местную ветвь анабаптизма, которая, без сомнения, была ревностной, но весьма склонной к хаосу и потрясениям.

К 1534 году напряжение от притока новых верующих достигло точки разлома, и анабаптистская церковь Нидерландов разделилась на два основных течения. Первое, возглавляемое братьями Филиппами — Дирком и Оббе, придерживалось новозаветного учения о разделении церкви и государства, а также непротивления. Это была церковь Менно Симонса и корень современных меннонитских общин.

Другое течение придерживалось более радикальных взглядов, возглавляемое Яном Маттисзом и Яном из Лейдена. Эти два человека становились всё более фанатичными в своих представлениях о возвращении Христа, веря, что они будут центральными фигурами, играющими ключевую роль в царстве, которое Бог установит на земле.

В то же время в обществе назревали беспокойства, которые вылились в город Мюнстер, расположенный на северо-западе Германии, где простые люди восстали, свергли городское правительство и изгнали католического епископа. Оба Яна быстро действовали, связавшись с новыми правителями города и в конечном итоге привлечя их на свою сторону.

Яны прибыли в Мюнстер в начале 1534 года и начали посылать пророков и вестников, призывавших всех «анабаптистов» собраться в этой «Новой Иерусалиме». Беспорядки в регионе делали их послание ещё более притягательным, и тысячи устремились в город, намереваясь стать частью этого апокалиптического пришествия Христа.

На горизонте действительно маячило апокалиптическое событие, но это было не возвращение Христа. Оно явилось в лице свергнутого католического епископа, который быстро осадил город. Его армия удерживала осаду в течение восемнадцати месяцев.

Внутри города Ян Маттисз, провозглашая видение, данное ему о спасении города, вышел за стены, чтобы пройтись в параде наружу, провозглашая скорую сдачу врага в его руки. Его видение, однако, подвело его: он был быстро схвачен врагом, обезглавлен, а его голова поставлена на пику перед воротами Мюнстера.

Внутри стен Ян из Лейдена взял на себя руководство, игнорируя голод, смерть и хаос, охватившие осаждённый город. Вместо чего он начал пропагандировать многожёнство, отстаивая его оправдание Ветхим Заветом, убил как минимум одну женщину, отказавшуюся выйти за него замуж, и в какой-то момент имел шестнадцать жён.

Это мерзостное деяние вскоре привело к ожидаемому концу: город был захвачен, и его жители подверглись жестоким расправам. Лидеры, наиболее заметным из которых был Ян из Лейдена, были схвачены, истязаемы и казнены. Их тела были подвешены в железных клетках на башне церкви Святого Ламберта, католического храма в Мюнстере. И по сей день эти клетки всё ещё висят, мрачное напоминание о гордости и опрометчивости двух Янов, полных решимости увидеть исполнение своего толкования о последних днях.

Во всех трёх этих примерах пророчества, содержащиеся в Божьем Слове, были искажены до таких последствий, которые отдалялись от воли Божьей к Его детям. Для евреев это привело к упущению Мессии, они не распознали величайшее обещание, данное им Богом. Христиане IV века, стеснённые ужасными гонениями Диоклетиана, приняли Константина как избавителя, видя в нём осуществление Божьего суда над царствами мира. Вместо мира они погрузились в состояние безбожия, худшее, чем у язычников вокруг них, и католическая церковь отклонилась в грехи, ужаснее даже их языческого общества. Наконец, тревожные видения и толкования менстеритов XVI века привели их к ужасной судьбе, опорочив имя истинной церкви.

Чему же мы должны научиться из этих тяжких ошибок предшествующих нам? В наше время конец кажется неотвратимым, и нас окружают те, кто убеждает, что мы поистине последние христиане.

Лука записал наставления Иисуса по этому вопросу: …Настанут дни, когда вы будете желать увидеть один из дней Сына Человеческого, и вы не увидите его. И скажут вам: вот здесь; или: там; не ходите и не бегите за ними — Luke 17:22-23. Здесь даны указания для нашего поведения в последние дни. Не будем бежать за слухами о конце времён, но будем послушны последнему наставлению нашего Господа — распространять Слово Божье и Евангелие Его Сына, Иисуса, по всему миру … и тогда придёт конец — Matthew 24:14.

Jesus, upon His ascension back into His heavenly home, gave a final directive to His disciples, both to those physically present as He disappeared into the clouds, and to the myriad of believers who would come to know Him down through the ages. The story of His life and His gospel were to be preached unto all the world by those who called Him Lord. This global spreading of the Word, would, in the later vision of John, be proclaimed as one of the prerequisites of Jesus’ triumphant return at the end of time. John himself would be seen as a harbinger of these end times, based on Jesus’ words as recorded by John … If I will that he [John] tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. John 21:22.

The early Christians, understandably, felt that the return of Christ was imminent, even within the first century. The rapid expansion of Christianity, the complete moral depravity of the Roman culture, and the increasing intensity of persecution against them seemed to point to a swift and triumphant return of their Lord.

Now, two thousand years since Christ gave that promise, His soon return seems just as imminent as it did to the first century believers. Speculation on the time of His return, the manner of it, and the contributing factors are always current and controversial subjects. In the light of this continued earnest expectation of the end times, what have we to learn about our interpretations of prophecy from those who have attempted to decipher the prophetic portions of Scripture in earlier ages?

Jesus' first coming was surrounded and enveloped by perhaps the most recognizable misinterpretation of prophecy in the Bible. Roughly four hundred years of relative silence from God precluded His entry into the world in a physical, human body. His birth would be unnoticed in a society that was not only in desperate need of, but also expecting, a Savior to arrive. Daniel, writing the words God gave him, had told of a Messiah to come, and had even given a time that He would appear. Now, the Jews seethed under Roman rule, hanging their hopes on what they thought would be a sudden and triumphant extermination of the Roman troops and influence from their lands. To us, it is glaringly obvious that their interpretation of prophecy was not only incorrect, but for many, would lead them astray so that they did not even recognize or acknowledge the true Redeemer that was sent to them.

But what was it that caused this misinterpreted view? To us, it seems completely in order that Jesus would focus on the poor and destitute rather than opposing an occupying army. Jewish historians give an intriguing, but scarcely surprising, answer to the failure of the majority of their people to recognize Christ for who He was.

The religious atmosphere of first century Israel was one defined by corruption, bribery, lust for power, and all the unsavory aspects of a completely politically motivated upper class.

The priests, once chosen by God to be His servants in sanctifying His children, had sunk to buying their positions of service, most notably in the high priest’s office, where God had ordained one high priest to serve the people throughout his life. In Jesus’ day, however, the responsibilities of leading the children of Israel were divvied out, the role often changing hands on one-year terms. Becoming a high priest was a matter of birth. Most high priests came from several large, influential, and wealthy families, as one often had to buy into the opportunity of this office.

It was not only the high priest’s office that was corrupted, but most levels of prominent spiritual leadership were filled by the wealthy elites who had the connections and wealth to be placed into roles of importance amongst the Jews.

This unsavory backdrop gives even more clarity to Jesus’ feelings on the religious leaders of His day. These imposters did not hold their priestly positions to serve His Father, they held them for their own gain, turning the temple into a marketplace and holding the common people hostage through their disputes on the minutiae of the Law.

Unsurprisingly, these leaders looked for a Messiah who would fit their goals, their ideals, and their morals, rather than one that would rebuke and chastise them for their hypocrisy, greed, and selfish ambition. Their view of prophecy had been so twisted and corrupted by their lifestyle that even the miracle of a resurrection could not sway them to view Christ’s power as coming from God. This misconstrued expectation of a conquering commander, riding a horse of war over the political enemies of these elites was pandered to the common Jew as well. Centuries of fighting for just the freedom to worship, as in the case of the Maccabees and the Greeks, had deeply imprinted a sense of nationalism into the collective mind of the Jewish people. The ones who bought into it the most were the ones who received the most from this system of exclusive access to God and His promises. To those who were repressed by the stringent and often man-made laws of Jewish society, a God of peace and love who would draw the needy of the world to Him was more welcome than a Saviour who would simply install another earthly government to rule the poor, oppress the widows, and reward the wicked.

This was not the last time an oppressed people would be deceived, as Roman rule would witness another major misstep in the collective interpretations of God’s people. This time, the teachings of Jesus and the words of His disciples would be misinterpreted to fit the changing political and religious landscape of fourth century Rome. The year was 306, and Diocletian, one of the most brutal persecutors of Christians in the Roman Empire, had abdicated from his position as Caesar. In his wake, he left three contenders for his throne. One of those vying for the seat of power was a young general, experienced in politics, and power hungry. His name was Constantine, son of a prominent Roman officer and a lowly Greek Christian, Helena.

From his youth, Constantine followed in his father’s footsteps, fighting throughout the empire, rising to a rank of general. Now, on campaign in Britain, he turned his eyes to the ultimate prize of a Roman politico, the title of Caesar, and the seat of the emperor.

Constantine’s line to the throne was through his father. Diocletian had, during his rule, appointed additional Caesars to aid in ruling the empire. Constantine’s father was one of these, and despite being simply appointed to the position, it was expected that his status as a Caesar would pass to his son. Matters were not as simple as a mere transfer of titles, however.

Constantine’s rise was bloody, but his grip on power was set, until he remained the sole contender for the throne. The stage was set. He quickly undid the harsh decrees of Diocletian, legalizing Christianity and removing the persecution that had leveled churches, scattered families, and hunted down bishops and other church leadership. Almost overnight, a peace previously unheard of was gifted to these hounded believers.

The changes that Constantine made did not end, however, with merely legalizing Christianity. His sympathies ran deeper, and he made further moves to legitimize it as not only an accepted religion, but as the state religion.

To Christians eager for the return of Christ, this seemed almost unbelievable. In the span of a few short years the government had gone from crucifying, beheading, and torturing them to holding them up as examples to the rest of the empire. The favor seems to have affected the clarity with which they viewed the apparent reconciliation of the world to the church. Not only would they accept a position of power in the empire, but they would also accept Constantine as a benefactor and protector of the church itself. In their minds, the day of the Lord was come, and Constantine was the rod of iron with which God would rule.

And rule he did. The course of the church was soon swayed by this new and outside influence. Constantine sat in on meetings of the bishops, even though at the time he was not baptized nor was he even seeking baptism. The church’s new position as a tool of the state brought schisms, in-fighting, and contention at every turn. There remained a remnant, but most of the church would fall under the sway of a man motivated by a hunger for power, wealth, and influence.

Constantine would be baptized before his death, lending him even further credibility in the eyes of a straying church. Now separated from its original identity as sheep in this world, the coming centuries would see “Christians” become ravening wolves, destroying, killing, and corrupting.

In a matter more recently related to us as Anabaptists, the tale of the infamous Muensterites gives us a further example of the perils of misinterpreting prophecy, especially the prophecy regarding the second coming of Christ.

One of the great disadvantages of a heavily persecuted group is a tendency to lack stability, as evidenced by the varying beliefs developed by Anabaptist groups of the movement's first fifty years. Persecution would deprive a congregation of their leaders, who were often those most targeted by the authorities. A missing elder meant less teaching, which in turn led to more difficulty in guidance, and corrective doctrine. Even the most sincere and interconnected groups could fall into errors developed because of the lack of leadership to bring Biblical clarity and balance the brotherhood.

The situation in the Netherlands was of a rather volatile strain approaching the 1530s. Throughout the country, the Catholic Church remained the predominant religion, clinging to their power through ruthless displays of physical force, most often directed towards the minority Protestant congregations. This focus on quelling the Protestant influence was momentarily successful in this instance, with most of their groups dissolving and reintegrating into the Catholic Church or other groups.

One of the groups that was on the receiving end of this minor diaspora was the fledging Dutch Anabaptist church. For those Protestants who still refused to join the Catholics, the Anabaptists often became their choice of church, rapidly swelling their ranks. This had a profound effect on the local strain of Anabaptism, which without a doubt was fervent, but quite prone to chaos and upheaval.

By 1534 the tensions of this influx of new believers reached a breaking point, and the Anabaptist church of the Netherlands split into two main factions. The first, led by the two Philips brothers, Dirk and Obbe, adhered to the New Testament teachings of separation from church and state, as well as nonresistance. This would be the church of Menno Simmons, and the root of the Mennonite churches of today.

The other faction held to more radical beliefs, led by Jan Matthysz and Jan of Leiden. These two men became increasingly fanatical in their views of Christ’s return, believing that they would be central figures, instrumental in a kingdom that God would set up on Earth.

At the same time, social unrest was brewing, and spilled over in the city of Munster, located in northwest Germany, where the common people rose up, overthrowing their city’s government and expelling their Catholic bishop. The two Jans were quick to act, contacting the new leaders of the city, and eventually winning them over to their views.

The Jans moved to Munser in early 1534, and began sending out prophets and messengers, who called all “Anabaptists” to congregate at this “New Jerusalem”. The unrest of the area made their message all the more appealing, and thousands streamed into the city, intent in being part of this apocalyptic return of Christ.

There was, in fact, an apocalyptic return on the horizon, but not a return of Christ. This one came in the form of the ousted Catholic bishop, who swiftly set siege to the city. His army would stay there for eighteen months.

Inside the city, Jan Matthysz, proclaiming a vision was given to him for a deliverance of the city, left its walls to parade outside, proclaiming a swift delivery of the enemy into his hands. His vision, however, failed him, as he was swiftly delivered into the hands of the enemy, where he was beheaded, and his head set on a pike in front Munster’s gates.

Inside the walls, Jan of Leiden took leadership, ignoring the famine, death, and chaos that now ran rampant within the besieged walls. Instead, he began promoting polygamy, defending it from the Old Testament, killing at least one woman who refused to marry him, and at one point, having sixteen wives.

This abomination soon led to its required end as the city was overcome, with a heavy slaughter being carried out against its inhabitants. The leaders, Jan of Leiden being the most prominent, were captured, tortured, and killed. Their bodies were hung in iron cages on the tower of St. Lamberts Church, the Catholic church in Munster. To this day, the cages still hang, a bleak reminder of the pride and rashness of the two Jans, determined to see their end-time interpretation fulfilled.

In all three of these examples, the prophecy contained in God’s Word was twisted into results that strayed far from the will of God for His children. For the Jews, it caused them to miss the Messiah, failing to recognize the greatest promise God had given them. The fourth century Christians, chafing under the horrific persecution of Diocletian, accepted Constantine as a deliverer, seeing him as a fulfillment of God’s judgement against the kingdoms of this world. Instead of peace, they would sink into a state of ungodliness worse than the pagans around them, with the Catholic Church straying into sin more horrible than even their pagan society. Lastly, the troubled visions and interpretations of the 16th century Munsterites would lead them to an awful fate, sullying the name of the true church.

What have we to learn from these grave errors of those before us? In our time, the end seems imminent, and we are beset with those who would have us believe that we are truly the last of the Christians.

Luke has recorded the instructions of Jesus on this point: …The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see it. And they shall say to you, See here; or, see there: go not after them, nor follow them –Luke 17: 22-23. Here are instructions for our conduct in the last days. Let us not be running after the rumors of the end times but let us be obedient to the final admonition of our Lord—that we spread the Word of God and the Gospel of His Son, Jesus throughout the world … and then shall the end come –Matthew 24:14.

Toen Jezus bij Zijn hemelvaart terugkeerde naar Zijn hemelse woonplaats, gaf Hij Zijn discipelen een laatste richtlijn, zowel aan degenen die fysiek aanwezig waren terwijl Hij in de wolken verdween, als aan de talloze gelovigen die Hem door de eeuwen heen zouden leren kennen. Het verhaal van Zijn leven en Zijn evangelie moesten door hen die Hem Heer noemden aan de hele wereld worden gepredikt. Deze wereldwijde verspreiding van het Woord zou, in de latere visie van Johannes, worden aangekondigd als een van de voorwaarden voor Jezus’ triomfantelijke terugkeer aan het einde der tijden. Johannes zelf zou, op grond van Jezus’ woorden zoals opgenomen door Johannes, worden gezien als een voorbode van deze eindtijd … If I will that he [John] tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. John 21:22.

De vroegste christenen voelden begrijpelijkerwijs dat de terugkeer van Christus nabij was, zelfs al in de eerste eeuw. De snelle uitbreiding van het christendom, de volledige morele verdering van de Romeinse cultuur en de toenemende intensiteit van de vervolging tegen hen leken te wijzen op een spoedige en triomfantelijke terugkeer van hun Heer.

Nu, tweeduizend jaar nadat Christus die belofte gaf, lijkt Zijn nabij terugkeer nog even imminent als voor de gelovigen van de eerste eeuw. Speculatie over het tijdstip van Zijn terugkeer, de wijze waarop die zal geschieden en de bijdragende factoren zijn voortdurend actuele en controversiële onderwerpen. In het licht van deze aanhoudende eerlijke verwachting van de eindtijd, wat leren wij over onze interpretaties van profetie van hen die in vroegere tijden hebben geprobeerd de profetische gedeelten van de Schrift te ontcijferen?

De eerste komst van Jezus werd omgeven en bedekt door misschien wel de meest herkenbare misinterpretatie van profetie in de Bijbel. Ongeveer vierhonderd jaren van relatieve stilte van God gingen vooraf aan Zijn intrede in de wereld in een fysiek, menselijk lichaam. Zijn geboorte zou onopgemerkt blijven in een samenleving die niet alleen wanhopig behoefte had aan, maar ook een Redder verwachtte. Daniël, die de woorden schreef die God hem gaf, had gesproken over een komende Messias en zelfs een tijd gegeven waarop Hij zou verschijnen. Nu broeiden de Joden onder Romeins bewind, en richtten hun hoop op wat zij dachten dat een plotselinge en triomfantelijke uitroeiing van de Romeinse troepen en invloed uit hun land zou zijn. Voor ons is het overduidelijk dat hun interpretatie van profetie niet alleen onjuist was, maar velen zou afleiden zodat ze de ware Verlosser die naar hen gezonden was niet eens herkenden of erkenden.

Maar wat veroorzaakte deze misbegrepen zienswijze? Het lijkt ons volkomen logisch dat Jezus zich zou richten op de armen en behoeftigen in plaats van het bezette leger te bestrijden. Joodse historici geven een intrigerend, maar weinig verrassend antwoord op het falen van de meerderheid van hun volk om Christus te herkennen zoals Hij was.

Het religieuze klimaat in Israël van de eerste eeuw werd gekenmerkt door corruptie, omkoping, machtswellust en alle onaangename aspecten van een volledig politiek gemotiveerde bovenlaag.

De priesters, eens door God gekozen om Zijn dienstknechten te zijn bij het heiligen van Zijn kinderen, waren gezonken tot het kopen van hun ambten, met name het hogepriesterlijk ambt, waar God had voorgeschreven dat één hogepriester gedurende zijn leven voor het volk zou dienen. In de dagen van Jezus werden echter de verantwoordelijkheden voor het leiden van de kinderen van Israël verdeeld, vaak met rollen die op jaarbasis van hand wisselden. Hogepriester worden was een kwestie van geboorte. De meeste hogepriesters kwamen uit enkele grote, invloedrijke en rijke families, aangezien men vaak moest 'inkopen' om in aanmerking te komen voor dit ambt.

Het was niet alleen het hogepriesterlijk ambt dat gecorrumpeerd was, maar de meeste niveaus van prominente geestelijke leiding werden vervuld door de rijke elites die de connecties en het vermogen hadden om in belangrijke rollen onder de Joden geplaatst te worden.

Deze onaangename achtergrond verduidelijkt des te meer Jezus’ gevoelens tegenover de religieuze leiders van Zijn tijd. Deze bedriegers hielden hun priesterlijke posities niet om Zijn Vader te dienen; zij hielden ze voor hun eigen gewin, maakten de tempel tot een marktplaats en hielden het gewone volk gegijzeld door hun geschillen over de kleinste details van de Wet.

Niet verrassend zochten deze leiders een Messias die in hun doelstellingen, idealen en normen paste, eerder dan een die hen terechtwees en tuchtigde vanwege hun huichelarij, hebzucht en egoïstische ambitie. Hun voorstelling van profetie was zo verdraaid en gecorrumpeerd door hun levenswijze dat zelfs het wonder van een opstanding hen er niet van kon overtuigen Christus’ kracht als afkomstig van God te zien. Deze verkeerd begrepen verwachting van een veroverende aanvoerder, rijdend op een oorlogspaard over de politieke vijanden van deze elites, werd ook aan de gewone Jood toegejuicht. Eeuwen van strijd voor slechts de vrijheid om te aanbidden, zoals in het geval van de Makkabeeën en de Grieken, hadden een gevoel van nationalisme diep in het collectieve bewustzijn van het Joodse volk geprent. Degenen die hier het meest in meegingen waren degenen die het meest ontvingen van dit systeem van exclusieve toegang tot God en Zijn beloften. Voor hen die onderdrukt werden door de strenge en vaak door mensen gemaakte wetten van de Joodse samenleving, was een God van vrede en liefde die de behoeftigen van de wereld naar Zich toe zou trekken meer welkom dan een Redder die simpelweg nog een aardse regering zou installeren om de armen te regeren, de weduwen te onderdrukken en de boosdoeners te belonen.

Dit was niet de laatste keer dat een onderdrukt volk werd misleid, want het Romeinse bewind zou getuige zijn van een andere grote misstap in de collectieve interpretaties van Gods volk. Dit keer zouden de leerstellingen van Jezus en de woorden van Zijn discipelen verkeerd geïnterpreteerd worden om te passen bij het veranderende politieke en religieuze landschap van het vierde-eeuwse Rome. Het jaar was 306, en Diocletianus, een van de wreedste vervolgers van christenen in het Romeinse Rijk, had afstand gedaan van zijn positie als Caesar. In zijn kielzog liet hij drie aanspraakmakers op zijn troon achter. Een van hen die streden om de machtszetel was een jonge generaal, ervaren in politiek en machtshongerig. Zijn naam was Constantijn, zoon van een prominente Romeinse officier en een eenvoudige Griekse christin, Helena.

Al vanaf zijn jeugd trad Constantijn in de voetsporen van zijn vader, vocht door het rijk heen en steeg tot de rang van generaal. Nu, tijdens een veldtocht in Brittannië, wendde hij zijn blik naar de ultieme prijs voor een Romeins politicus: de titel van Caesar en de zetel van de keizer.

Constantijns aanspraak op de troon liep via zijn vader. Diocletianus had tijdens zijn bewind extra Caesars aangesteld om te helpen bij het besturen van het rijk. Constantijns vader was een van hen, en hoewel hij louter aangesteld was, werd verwacht dat zijn status als Caesar op zijn zoon zou overgaan. De zaken waren echter niet zo simpel als een loutere overdracht van titels.

Constantijns opkomst was bloedig, maar zijn greep op de macht werd gevestigd, totdat hij de enige overgeblevene was die aanspraak maakte op de troon. Het toneel was gereed. Hij wierp snel de harde decreten van Diocletianus terug, legaliseerde het christendom en nam de vervolging weg die kerken had verwoest, families had verspreid en bisschoppen en andere kerkelijke leiders had opgejaagd. Bijna van de ene op de andere dag viel er een tot dan toe ongekende vrede te beurt aan deze geplaagde gelovigen.

De veranderingen die Constantijn doorvoerde hielden echter niet op bij het louter legaliseren van het christendom. Zijn sympathieën gingen dieper, en hij nam verdere maatregelen om het niet alleen als een geaccepteerde religie te legitimeren, maar als de staatsgodsdienst.

Voor christenen die verlangden naar de terugkeer van Christus, leek dit bijna ongelooflijk. In enkele jaren was de overheid gegaan van het kruisigen, onthoofden en martelen van hen naar het uitstreken van hen als voorbeelden voor de rest van het rijk. Die gunst schijnbaar beïnvloedde de helderheid waarmee zij de schijnbare verzoening van de wereld met de kerk bekeken. Niet alleen accepteerden zij een positie van macht in het rijk, zij accepteerden ook Constantijn als weldoener en beschermer van de kerk zelf. In hun gedachten was de dag des Heren gekomen en was Constantijn de IJzeren staf waarmee God zou regeren.

En regeren deed hij. De koers van de kerk zou spoedig door deze nieuwe en externe invloed worden beïnvloed. Constantijn woonde bijeenkomsten van de bisschoppen bij, hoewel hij op dat moment niet gedoopt was en zelfs niet naar doop zocht. De nieuwe positie van de kerk als instrument van de staat bracht scheuringen, onderlinge strijd en onenigheid bij elke stap. Er bleef een overblijfsel, maar het grootste deel van de kerk zou onder de invloed komen van een man gemotiveerd door honger naar macht, rijkdom en aanzien.

Constantijn zou voor zijn dood gedoopt worden, hetgeen hem nog meer geloofwaardigheid gaf in de ogen van een afvallige kerk. Nu gescheiden van haar oorspronkelijke identiteit als schapen in deze wereld, zouden de komende eeuwen zien hoe “christenen” veranderden in razende wolven, die vernietigden, doodden en verrotte.

Meer recentelijk, en verbonden met ons als wederdoopgezinden, geeft het verhaal van de beruchte Munsterieten ons een verder voorbeeld van de gevaren van het verkeerd interpreteren van profetie, vooral de profetie betreffende de wederkomst van Christus.

Een van de grote nadelen van een ernstig vervolgde groep is een neiging tot gebrek aan stabiliteit, zoals blijkt uit de uiteenlopende overtuigingen die zich ontwikkelden onder de wederdopers in de eerste vijftig jaar van de beweging. Vervolging zou een gemeente haar leiders ontnemen, die vaak degenen waren die het meest door de autoriteiten werden opgejaagd. Een ontbrekende ouderling betekende minder onderwijs, wat op zijn beurt leidde tot meer moeilijkheden bij leiding en corrigerende leer. Zelfs de meest oprechte en onderling verbonden groepen konden in dwalingen vervallen die ontstonden door het gebrek aan leiderschap dat Bijbelse duidelijkheid en balans aan de broederschap zou brengen.

De situatie in de Nederlanden was van een tamelijk explosieve soort toen de jaren 1530 naderden. In het hele land bleef de Katholieke Kerk de overheersende religie, die haar macht vasthield door meedogenloze vertoningen van fysieke dwang, meestal gericht tegen de minderheidsgroeperingen van protestantse gemeenten. Deze focus op het onderdrukken van de protestantse invloed had in dit geval even succes, waarbij de meeste van hun groepen uiteenvielen en opnieuw opgingen in de Katholieke Kerk of andere groeperingen.

Een van de groepen die het slachtoffer werd van deze kleine diaspora was de opkomende Nederlandse wederdoperskerk. Voor die protestanten die nog weigerden zich bij de katholieken aan te sluiten, werden de wederdopers vaak hun keuze van kerk, waardoor hun gelederen snel aangroeiden. Dit had een diepgaande invloed op de lokale stroming van het wederdoperschap, dat zonder twijfel vurig was, maar erg vatbaar voor chaos en omwenteling.

In 1534 bereikten de spanningen door deze instroom van nieuwe gelovigen een breekpunt en splitste de wederdoperskerk in de Nederlanden zich in twee hoofdfracties. De eerste, geleid door de twee Philips-broers, Dirk en Obbe, hield vast aan de leer van het Nieuwe Testament over scheiding van kerk en staat, evenals nonresistentie. Dit zou de kerk van Menno Simons zijn en de wortel van de hedendaagse doopsgezinde kerken.

De andere factie hield aan radicalere opvattingen vast, geleid door Jan Matthysz en Jan van Leiden. Deze twee mannen werden steeds fanatieker in hun opvattingen over Christus’ terugkeer en geloofden dat zij centrale figuren zouden zijn, instrumenteel in een koninkrijk dat God op aarde zou vestigen.

Terwijl dit speelde, broeide er sociale onrust die uitbarstte in de stad Münster, gelegen in het noordwesten van Duitsland, waar het gewone volk in opstand kwam, de regering van hun stad omverwierp en hun katholieke bisschop verdreef. De twee Jans waren snel ter plaatse, namen contact op met de nieuwe leiders van de stad en wonnen hen uiteindelijk voor hun zienswijzen.

De Jans verhuisden begin 1534 naar Münster en begonnen profeten en boodschappers uit te zenden die alle “wederdopers” opriepen zich te verzamelen in dit “Nieuwe Jeruzalem”. De onrust in de regio maakte hun boodschap des te aantrekkelijker en duizenden stroomden de stad binnen, vastbesloten deel uit te maken van deze apocalyptische terugkeer van Christus.

Er was inderdaad een apocalyptische terugkeer aan de horizon, maar het was niet de terugkeer van Christus. Deze kwam in de gedaante van de verdreven katholieke bisschop, die snel de stad belegerde. Zijn leger zou daar achttien maanden blijven.

Binnen de stad verliet Jan Matthysz, die beweerde een visioen te hebben gekregen over de bevrijding van de stad, de muren om buiten te paraderen en de snelle overgave van de vijand te verkondigen. Zijn visioen liet hem echter in de steek, want hij werd snel in handen van de vijand gegeven, onthoofd en zijn hoofd op een spies voor de poorten van Münster gezet.

Binnen de muren nam Jan van Leiden het leiderschap op zich en negeerde de hongersnood, de dood en de chaos die nu in de belegerde stad heersten. In plaats daarvan begon hij polygamie te promoten, verdedigde hij die vanuit het Oude Testament, doodde ten minste één vrouw die weigerde met hem te trouwen en had hij op een gegeven moment zestien vrouwen.

Deze gruwel leidde spoedig tot het onvermijdelijke einde toen de stad werd ingenomen en er een zware slachting onder de inwoners plaatsvond. De leiders, met Jan van Leiden als de meest prominente, werden gevangen genomen, gefolterd en gedood. Hun lichamen werden in ijzeren kooien aan de toren van de St. Lambertskerk, de katholieke kerk in Münster, gehangen. Tot op de dag van vandaag hangen die kooien er nog, een donkere herinnering aan de trots en overhaastheid van de twee Jans, vastbesloten hun eindtijdinterpretatie vervuld te zien.

In al deze drie voorbeelden werd de profetie vervormd tot uitkomsten die ver afweken van Gods wil voor Zijn kinderen. Voor de Joden veroorzaakte het dat zij de Messias misten en faalden de grootste belofte die God hun had gegeven te herkennen. De christenen van de vierde eeuw, gekweld door de afschuwelijke vervolging onder Diocletianus, accepteerden Constantijn als een verlosser en zagen hem als een vervulling van Gods oordeel over de koninkrijken van deze wereld. In plaats van vrede zouden zij zinken in een goddeloosheid die erger was dan die van de heidenen om hen heen, waarbij de Katholieke Kerk afweek in zonden nog afschuwelijker dan die van hun heidense samenleving. Ten slotte leidden de verontrustende visioenen en interpretaties van de Münsterieten in de 16e eeuw hen tot een verschrikkelijk lot en bezoedelden zij de naam van de ware kerk.

Wat moeten wij leren van deze ernstige fouten van hen vóór ons? In onze tijd lijkt het einde nabij, en worden wij omringd door hen die ons willen doen geloven dat wij werkelijk de laatsten van de christenen zijn.

Lukas heeft de instructies van Jezus over dit punt opgetekend: …The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see it. And they shall say to you, See here; or, see there: go not after them, nor follow them –Luke 17: 22-23. Hierin staan aanwijzingen voor ons gedrag in de laatste dagen. Laten we niet achter de geruchten over de eindtijd aanrennen, maar gehoorzaam zijn aan de laatste vermaning van onze Heer—dat wij het Woord van God en het Evangelie van Zijn Zoon, Jezus, over de gehele wereld verspreiden … and then shall the end come –Matthew 24:14.

I watched as a man attempted to cut a large sheet of plywood in half. He was talking with a few other men while he was cutting, and it seemed that he wasn’t too concerned about making the cut straight. I noticed that he continued to cut further and further from the line that he had scratched into the piece of plywood with a nail. After he was several inches off, one of his friends tried to point it out but he pretended to ignore him. He tried to casually guide the old handsaw back towards the line, while continuing to talk with the men, not making a big deal of it. Finally, after he was more than a foot off, he stopped. He knew now that he had a problem, a problem he could not fix.

I had to think, “Is this what we are doing as the church, the bride of Christ?” We are not too serious about drifting off the straight and narrow way; we allow things to come into our midst. We say, “It’s not a big deal, let’s not be critical.” But the longer we wait, the harder it will be to straighten out. At first it shocks us; later it becomes the new normal. How do we tell if we have drifted? It should be as easy as considering where we used to be, and comparing it that with where we are now, then evaluating the change with what the Bible teaches.

Since fighting against drift is not popular, men in the church don’t want to do it. Some people in our churches who are drifting towards the world have perfected a feel-good gospel. They go on and on about how close they are getting to Jesus, and how blessed they are, but their direction is clearly not in line with the teachings of Scripture. They’re headed towards the world.

There are others who don’t want the church to drift, yet they have their own problems—the love of money, covetousness, and a love of pleasure. No one says anything because it seems that nobody wants to hear. A popular response is, “Yes, I know it’s not good, but what can we do?” “All churches have problems.” Or “Yes, I would never allow that, but I don’t feel it’s in my place to speak up about it.” “It’s not for my family, but if others want to do that, its fine.”

We live in a “me” age. Everything is about me. The conservative, Anabaptist people are getting tangled up in social media, selfies, tweeting, Facebook, and you name it. We love ourselves to the extent that we talk, act, and dress in ways that draw attention to ourselves—we promote ourselves. We talk about looking good, feeling good, and living good. What happened to promoting Jesus? Remember, Jesus said: For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it –Matthew 16:25.

Why does it seem so hard to tell which direction we are going? If we are all about ourselves, then we are not all about Jesus. If we are into the latest fashions and the nicest cars, trucks, and houses, then we are not all about Jesus. We cannot indulge ourselves in pleasing the flesh, and still say we are Christians.

I was recently asked why some pastors lose their children to the world. In most cases, I believe it’s the same reason that many Anabaptists are losing their children to the kingdom of darkness—the fathers have lost a godly vision for their homes. They live a powerless life and allow the world to come in. Maybe they do not have television, but what about the internet? This still allows the influence of the world to come in. Also, Dad spends more time with his business and more time enjoying life than he does seeking the face of God.

Many Americans go on short-term missions. Many times, it seems that the youth who go want to hit the beach or some other pleasure and relaxation as soon as they get off the plane. Why? Because that’s what they are either taught or allowed to do back home—seek pleasure. They haven’t been taught to deny the flesh; they haven’t seen their parents deny the flesh. Some of us might be so far off the mark that we need to do like the carpenter at the beginning of this article—Humble ourselves and start over.

Husbands are pulling their unwilling wives into the world, wives are pushing their husbands into the world, and children are dragging their parents into the world. And unfortunately, since the modern church has thrown off all forms of discipline and structure, everyone can stay in the church and pollute it with their worldly ideas (at least as long as you smile and say you love Jesus.) Remember the Scriptures: If ye love me, keep my commandments –John 14:15. And, He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him –1 John 2:4.

Here are some areas of drift in the church.

Brotherly love

By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another –John 13:35.

People have visited our church and asked if we practice the holy kiss. I reply that we do; however, understanding the need to love one another comes first. Many churches are doing away with the holy kiss, which is clearly instructed in the Word. And it seems appropriate because they have stopped loving one another. I don’t believe we understand the importance of this topic—having love one for another. When our love causes us to suffer for one another, the world sees it. Often, the reason a brotherhood stops loving each other is because they are not in the fight “together” anymore. They have become independent.

Some of the greatest acts of showing love for one another have happened on the battlefield. Men have jumped on grenades, and they have jumped in front of bullets to save their comrades. Because they have fought together, they look out for each other. What if a soldier marching out to battle would notice a fellow soldier’s ammunition clip fall from his gun? What would he do? Would he remain quiet because his comrade might get mad? Or would he remain quiet because he knew that he had his own problems? No. He would help his brother. If ungodly men on the battlefield can practice this, why can’t God’s people do so in the church? Before I was converted, I was in the military. I chose to suffer for my country. Now that I’m a Christian, I now choose to suffer for my Lord.

Dress

This is the most obvious, but also the most overlooked. The worldly church says, “It’s the heart that counts, so how we appear on the outside doesn’t matter”. Are the Anabaptists falling for this? The world used to dress modestly, but television and Hollywood began to promote a focus on the human body. Surely the church wouldn’t follow Hollywood. But what is the difference—a woman of the world who is obviously dressed immodestly, or a woman of the church dressed with a cape dress that is form-fitting, and with a little covering hanging skimpily on the back of her head? There is little difference, except the one claims to be a Christian and the other one doesn’t. Dear ones, the world is laughing at us.

So how does it all start? Subtly. First remove a pleat here or a gather there, then start using a little less material, finally, start buying brighter bolder colors. The men untuck the shirt, switch to jeans, then skinny jeans, undo a few buttons, grow out the hair a little. Buy a pair of the “cool” name brand shoes, and a cowboy hat. The devil is no fool. If you drop a frog into boiling water, it will jump out quickly. If you boil the water that contains the frog, he will slowly cook to death. Is it too late for us to jump out? With God all things are possible. Brothers and sisters, it is the heart that counts; and if we desire to look like the world, our heart is worldly and needs to be cleaned—cleaned by the ever so powerful blood of Jesus.

Pleasure

Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter. Ye have condemned and killed the just; and he doth not resist you –James 5:5-6.

And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection –Luke 8:14.

This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away –2 Timothy 3:1-5.

When we are given to pleasure, we separate ourselves from the sufferings we have been called to, therefore separating us from the reward received from suffering.

Remember, when we give in a little on any issue during our generation, our children will go farther with it. When our children enjoy going to church only because of the volleyball game that’s scheduled afterward, it’s not good. When they want to go on a mission trip because of the pleasures of the ocean, it’s not good. I’m not saying those things are bad, but when they become the focal point, we have a serious problem. Do we enjoy doing the things that God enjoys? Do we enjoy hymn sings anymore? Do we enjoy helping the poor? What about visiting the widows? I believe if the fathers have their priorities right, and they truly love doing the things of God even if the flesh suffers, then so will our children, (the next generation) for which WE are responsible. I often tell people that they don’t need to follow Jesus. They can love the world, and the pleasures of this life, but they cannot continue sitting in our church and pretend they are Christians. People might say that’s too harsh, but I believe Jesus said the same thing. I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth –Revelation 3:15-16.

This is not a complete list as there are many other ways that the church is drifting towards the world. My prayer is that, first, we could see the problem, and second, we could deal with it. Remember a little leaven leavens the lump. (1 Corinthians 5)

There is a battle that’s raging; the kingdom of darkness is pressing in. The devil truly knows he has but a short time. Let us make a stand, put down our white flags, and pick up our swords. Let us remove the traitors, the world, and the sin that has come into the church. Let us purify the church and fight the good fight of faith.

How do we stop the drift? How do we leave behind a faithful generation? First, the fathers need to teach their children, and the leaders in the church need to teach them all. The early Anabaptists met as many times as they could, and that was usually out in the weather, in some woods somewhere. Our church here meets five times a week. Meeting on Sundays only, I believe, shows where our priorities are.

And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: – Ephesians 4:11-13.

It seems that God would give us teachers, pastors, evangelists, prophets, and apostles if we would use them.

Let’s make this personal—there could be areas of drift in my life. We need to help each other before we all drift into ruin. Maybe we can maintain, but we also need to be concerned about our children. If we could get together and be honest with ourselves and with one another about what the scriptures clearly teach, then we would be more careful. If we could study God’s Word together, with open hearts and minds, I believe we could strengthen that which remains. I believe if we would fall on our faces before God, He would heal our churches. May God bless us all in a deeper walk with Him.
