„Mensch, ist das warm!“ rief Mama aus. „Ein richtig guter Regen würde uns guttun, damit es ein bisschen abkühlt.“

Es war Samstag, gegen Ende Juni, und das Wetter war an diesem Tag besonders heiß und schwül gewesen. Ellies Mutter hatte das Haus geputzt und etwas Essen vorbereitet für die Gäste, die am Sonntag nach dem Gottesdienst zum Mittagessen kommen sollten.

Als der Nachmittag in den frühen Abend überging, schien es noch heißer zu werden, und es war kein Lüftchen zu spüren. Ellies Vater ruhte in einer Hängematte auf dem Rasen, während der Rest der Familie versuchte, den angenehmsten Platz zu finden, um sich von der Hitze zu befreien.

Gegen Abend zogen dann Wolken auf. Sie kamen plötzlich, begleitet von Böen, die den Staub aufzuwirbeln begannen. Blitze zuckten über den Himmel, und in der Ferne rollte Donner.

„Schnell, Kinder!“ rief Mama. „Räumt eure Spielsachen weg; es wird gleich stürmen!“

Ellie sah alarmiert um sich. Es wurde sehr schnell dunkel und der Himmel sah merkwürdig—fast wütend—aus. Sie sammelte rasch ihre Spielsachen ein und eilte ins Haus. Papa schlief nicht mehr in der Hängematte. Der Wind hatte sie fast umgerissen und ihn gleich mit! Auch er hastete ins Haus; der Wind ließ die Tür heftig zuschlagen. Die Familie versammelte sich auf der Veranda, um den herannahenden Sturm zu beobachten. Nach Westen und Süden gab es Fenster, so dass sie einen guten Überblick über den kommenden Regen hatten. Der Wind blies mit einer Kraft, die Ellie in ihren sieben Jahren noch nie erlebt hatte. Sie bemerkte die Besorgnis und die Angst in den Gesichtern ihrer Eltern, während sie zusahen und warteten.

Dann begann es zu regnen. Große Regenbänder peitschten gegen die Fenster, und Ellie fragte sich, ob der Regen stark genug sein könnte, um das Glas zu zerbrechen.

„Was war das?“ rief Mama, als plötzlich ein Blechdach entlang der Veranda vorbeisauste und jenseits des Gartens verschwand.

„Ich glaube, das ist ein Teil vom Garagendach,“ sagte Papa ungläubig, während er vorsichtig durch die Fenster spähte.

Als Mama das hörte, wies sie die Kinder an, sich an die Kellertür zu stellen. Falls es schlimmer würde, sollten sie hinuntergehen! Ellie hatte große Angst. Was würde mit ihnen geschehen? Würde ihr Haus wegfliegen? Würde jemand verletzt werden?

So abrupt wie der Sturm begonnen hatte, legte er sich wieder. Der Wind ließ nach, der Regen wurde schwächer, und sehr bald schien wieder die Sonne. Die Familie wagte sich vorsichtig nach draußen, um zu sehen, was während des Sturms alles passiert war.

„Schaut!“ sagte Papa. „Das Garagendach ist weg und die Südwand auch!“

„Warum sieht Geralds Haus so komisch aus?“ zeigte Mama auf die Nachbarn nebenan. „Sieh mal! Das ganze Dach ist von ihrem Haus verschwunden!“ In der Tat war das Dach sauber abgerissen worden, und die Giebel standen dort stumm da, ohne etwas zu tragen.

In der Ferne waren Sirenen zu hören, und als sie sich in der Nachbarschaft umsahen, konnten sie Rauch hinter einigen Bäumen erkennen.

„Das muss Melvins Scheune sein, die brennt!“ rief Papa. „Ich gehe sehen, ob ich helfen kann.“ Er stürmte zu seinem Pickup und fuhr bald die Auffahrt hinunter.

Der Wind war so stark gewesen, dass einige Strommasten umgeweht wurden und der Strom abgeschaltet war, sodass es weder Licht noch Ventilatoren gab. Nachdem der Sturm vorüber war, kehrten die Schwüle und Hitze zurück, sodass die Nacht heiß und drückend blieb. Doch die Erwachsenen aus der Gegend arbeiteten bis tief in die Nacht hinein zusammen, halfen einander und räumten so viel Sturm‑Schaden weg, wie sie konnten.

Besonders betroffen war unser Nachbar Melvin. Seine Scheune war auf dutzende Rinder eingestürzt und dann hatte ein Brand ausgebrochen. Die Männer aus der Nachbarschaft versuchten verzweifelt, die Rinder zu retten, die sie noch retten konnten, aber am Ende konnten viele der Ochsen nicht gerettet werden.

Der Sonntag kam, aber niemand ging in die Kirche. Der Morgen wurde bei Melvin verbracht, totes Vieh wegzufahren, verbranntes Heu zu beseitigen und einfach füreinander da zu sein. Es war harte, schwere Arbeit. Ellie erinnert sich deutlich daran, wie schrecklich der Geruch war. Und sie konnte sich kaum dazu bringen, zuzusehen, wie die toten Ochsen aufgeladen wurden. Als die Mittagszeit kam, trafen die Gäste ein, aber niemand hatte großen Appetit. Ellies kleiner Bruder schluchzte: „Ich kann nur an diese armen Ochsen denken!“

Ellie war überrascht, wie gewaltig ein Sturm sein konnte. Und furchterregend! Würden sie noch einmal einen Tornado erleben? Könnten noch mehr Gebäude einstürzen, und könnte noch eine Scheune oder ein Haus niederbrennen? In Ellies Herz begann ein Samen der Angst zu wachsen. Im Verlauf jenes Sommers und vieler Sommer danach, jedes Mal, wenn Donner grollte oder sie die Worte „Tornado‑Warnung“ hörte, schlug ihr Herz schneller und ein Knoten setzte sich in ihrem Magen fest. Wie sie jeden Sturm fürchtete! Sie wünschte sich, sie würden alle einfach an ihrem Haus vorüberziehen. Warum ließ Gott eigentlich Stürme zu?

„Du musst Gott vertrauen, Ellie“, sagte ihre Mutter. „Er ist derjenige, der das Wetter gemacht hat, und er hat alles unter seiner Kontrolle. Er hält uns vielleicht nicht immer davon fern, erschreckende Zeiten zu erleben, aber er ist immer da, um für uns zu sorgen.“

Als sie älter wurde, lernte Ellie, diesen Rat sich zu Herzen zu nehmen. Ihre Angst vor Stürmen ließ nach, und an ihre Stelle trat eine Faszination dafür, wie Stürme entstehen und sich bilden. Zu wissen, dass Gott der Herr des Windes ist, ist ihr immer noch ein Trost und eine Zusicherung. Vor allem hat sie, indem sie gelernt hat, Gott in jedem Bereich ihres Lebens zu vertrauen, ihn stets als treu erfahren. Zu lernen, Angst durch Vertrauen zu ersetzen, bringt dem Herzen immer Frieden.

I watched as a man attempted to cut a large sheet of plywood in half. He was talking with a few other men while he was cutting, and it seemed that he wasn’t too concerned about making the cut straight. I noticed that he continued to cut further and further from the line that he had scratched into the piece of plywood with a nail. After he was several inches off, one of his friends tried to point it out but he pretended to ignore him. He tried to casually guide the old handsaw back towards the line, while continuing to talk with the men, not making a big deal of it. Finally, after he was more than a foot off, he stopped. He knew now that he had a problem, a problem he could not fix.

I had to think, “Is this what we are doing as the church, the bride of Christ?” We are not too serious about drifting off the straight and narrow way; we allow things to come into our midst. We say, “It’s not a big deal, let’s not be critical.” But the longer we wait, the harder it will be to straighten out. At first it shocks us; later it becomes the new normal. How do we tell if we have drifted? It should be as easy as considering where we used to be, and comparing it that with where we are now, then evaluating the change with what the Bible teaches.

Since fighting against drift is not popular, men in the church don’t want to do it. Some people in our churches who are drifting towards the world have perfected a feel-good gospel. They go on and on about how close they are getting to Jesus, and how blessed they are, but their direction is clearly not in line with the teachings of Scripture. They’re headed towards the world.

There are others who don’t want the church to drift, yet they have their own problems—the love of money, covetousness, and a love of pleasure. No one says anything because it seems that nobody wants to hear. A popular response is, “Yes, I know it’s not good, but what can we do?” “All churches have problems.” Or “Yes, I would never allow that, but I don’t feel it’s in my place to speak up about it.” “It’s not for my family, but if others want to do that, its fine.”

We live in a “me” age. Everything is about me. The conservative, Anabaptist people are getting tangled up in social media, selfies, tweeting, Facebook, and you name it. We love ourselves to the extent that we talk, act, and dress in ways that draw attention to ourselves—we promote ourselves. We talk about looking good, feeling good, and living good. What happened to promoting Jesus? Remember, Jesus said: For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it –Matthew 16:25.

Why does it seem so hard to tell which direction we are going? If we are all about ourselves, then we are not all about Jesus. If we are into the latest fashions and the nicest cars, trucks, and houses, then we are not all about Jesus. We cannot indulge ourselves in pleasing the flesh, and still say we are Christians.

I was recently asked why some pastors lose their children to the world. In most cases, I believe it’s the same reason that many Anabaptists are losing their children to the kingdom of darkness—the fathers have lost a godly vision for their homes. They live a powerless life and allow the world to come in. Maybe they do not have television, but what about the internet? This still allows the influence of the world to come in. Also, Dad spends more time with his business and more time enjoying life than he does seeking the face of God.

Many Americans go on short-term missions. Many times, it seems that the youth who go want to hit the beach or some other pleasure and relaxation as soon as they get off the plane. Why? Because that’s what they are either taught or allowed to do back home—seek pleasure. They haven’t been taught to deny the flesh; they haven’t seen their parents deny the flesh. Some of us might be so far off the mark that we need to do like the carpenter at the beginning of this article—Humble ourselves and start over.

Husbands are pulling their unwilling wives into the world, wives are pushing their husbands into the world, and children are dragging their parents into the world. And unfortunately, since the modern church has thrown off all forms of discipline and structure, everyone can stay in the church and pollute it with their worldly ideas (at least as long as you smile and say you love Jesus.) Remember the Scriptures: If ye love me, keep my commandments –John 14:15. And, He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him –1 John 2:4.

Here are some areas of drift in the church.

Brotherly love

By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another –John 13:35.

People have visited our church and asked if we practice the holy kiss. I reply that we do; however, understanding the need to love one another comes first. Many churches are doing away with the holy kiss, which is clearly instructed in the Word. And it seems appropriate because they have stopped loving one another. I don’t believe we understand the importance of this topic—having love one for another. When our love causes us to suffer for one another, the world sees it. Often, the reason a brotherhood stops loving each other is because they are not in the fight “together” anymore. They have become independent.

Some of the greatest acts of showing love for one another have happened on the battlefield. Men have jumped on grenades, and they have jumped in front of bullets to save their comrades. Because they have fought together, they look out for each other. What if a soldier marching out to battle would notice a fellow soldier’s ammunition clip fall from his gun? What would he do? Would he remain quiet because his comrade might get mad? Or would he remain quiet because he knew that he had his own problems? No. He would help his brother. If ungodly men on the battlefield can practice this, why can’t God’s people do so in the church? Before I was converted, I was in the military. I chose to suffer for my country. Now that I’m a Christian, I now choose to suffer for my Lord.

Dress

This is the most obvious, but also the most overlooked. The worldly church says, “It’s the heart that counts, so how we appear on the outside doesn’t matter”. Are the Anabaptists falling for this? The world used to dress modestly, but television and Hollywood began to promote a focus on the human body. Surely the church wouldn’t follow Hollywood. But what is the difference—a woman of the world who is obviously dressed immodestly, or a woman of the church dressed with a cape dress that is form-fitting, and with a little covering hanging skimpily on the back of her head? There is little difference, except the one claims to be a Christian and the other one doesn’t. Dear ones, the world is laughing at us.

So how does it all start? Subtly. First remove a pleat here or a gather there, then start using a little less material, finally, start buying brighter bolder colors. The men untuck the shirt, switch to jeans, then skinny jeans, undo a few buttons, grow out the hair a little. Buy a pair of the “cool” name brand shoes, and a cowboy hat. The devil is no fool. If you drop a frog into boiling water, it will jump out quickly. If you boil the water that contains the frog, he will slowly cook to death. Is it too late for us to jump out? With God all things are possible. Brothers and sisters, it is the heart that counts; and if we desire to look like the world, our heart is worldly and needs to be cleaned—cleaned by the ever so powerful blood of Jesus.

Pleasure

Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter. Ye have condemned and killed the just; and he doth not resist you –James 5:5-6.

And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection –Luke 8:14.

This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away –2 Timothy 3:1-5.

When we are given to pleasure, we separate ourselves from the sufferings we have been called to, therefore separating us from the reward received from suffering.

Remember, when we give in a little on any issue during our generation, our children will go farther with it. When our children enjoy going to church only because of the volleyball game that’s scheduled afterward, it’s not good. When they want to go on a mission trip because of the pleasures of the ocean, it’s not good. I’m not saying those things are bad, but when they become the focal point, we have a serious problem. Do we enjoy doing the things that God enjoys? Do we enjoy hymn sings anymore? Do we enjoy helping the poor? What about visiting the widows? I believe if the fathers have their priorities right, and they truly love doing the things of God even if the flesh suffers, then so will our children, (the next generation) for which WE are responsible. I often tell people that they don’t need to follow Jesus. They can love the world, and the pleasures of this life, but they cannot continue sitting in our church and pretend they are Christians. People might say that’s too harsh, but I believe Jesus said the same thing. I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth –Revelation 3:15-16.

This is not a complete list as there are many other ways that the church is drifting towards the world. My prayer is that, first, we could see the problem, and second, we could deal with it. Remember a little leaven leavens the lump. (1 Corinthians 5)

There is a battle that’s raging; the kingdom of darkness is pressing in. The devil truly knows he has but a short time. Let us make a stand, put down our white flags, and pick up our swords. Let us remove the traitors, the world, and the sin that has come into the church. Let us purify the church and fight the good fight of faith.

How do we stop the drift? How do we leave behind a faithful generation? First, the fathers need to teach their children, and the leaders in the church need to teach them all. The early Anabaptists met as many times as they could, and that was usually out in the weather, in some woods somewhere. Our church here meets five times a week. Meeting on Sundays only, I believe, shows where our priorities are.

And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: – Ephesians 4:11-13.

It seems that God would give us teachers, pastors, evangelists, prophets, and apostles if we would use them.

Let’s make this personal—there could be areas of drift in my life. We need to help each other before we all drift into ruin. Maybe we can maintain, but we also need to be concerned about our children. If we could get together and be honest with ourselves and with one another about what the scriptures clearly teach, then we would be more careful. If we could study God’s Word together, with open hearts and minds, I believe we could strengthen that which remains. I believe if we would fall on our faces before God, He would heal our churches. May God bless us all in a deeper walk with Him.

Ik keek toe hoe een man probeerde een groot stuk multiplex in tweeën te zagen. Hij praatte met een paar andere mannen terwijl hij aan het zagen was, en het leek alsof hij niet erg bekommerd was om de zaagsnede recht te maken. Ik merkte dat hij steeds verder van de lijn af bleef zagen die hij met een nagel in het stuk multiplex had gekrast. Nadat hij enkele inches mis zat, probeerde een van zijn vrienden het aan te wijzen, maar hij deed alsof hij het negeerde. Hij probeerde de oude handzaag nonchalant weer naar de lijn te leiden, terwijl hij met de mannen bleef praten, zonder er een groot ding van te maken. Uiteindelijk, nadat hij meer dan een voet ernaast zat, stopte hij. Hij wist nu dat hij een probleem had, een probleem dat hij niet kon herstellen.

Ik moest denken: "Is dit wat wij doen als de kerk, de bruid van Christus?" We nemen het afdwalen van de rechte en smalle weg niet te serieus; we laten dingen in onze midden komen. We zeggen: "Het is niet zo erg, laten we niet kritisch zijn." Maar hoe langer we wachten, hoe moeilijker het zal zijn om het recht te buigen. Eerst schrikt het ons; later wordt het de nieuwe normaal. Hoe kunnen we zien of we zijn afgedreven? Het zou zo eenvoudig moeten zijn door te overwegen waar we vroeger waren, dat te vergelijken met waar we nu zijn, en de verandering te beoordelen aan de hand van wat de Bijbel leert.

Aangezien het bestrijden van afglijden niet populair is, willen mannen in de kerk het niet doen. Sommige mensen in onze kerken die naar de wereld afdruiven, hebben een prettig-voelend evangelie geperfectioneerd. Ze blijven maar praten over hoe dicht ze bij Jezus komen en hoe gezegend ze zijn, maar hun koers is duidelijk niet in overeenstemming met de leer van de Schrift. Ze gaan richting de wereld.

Er zijn anderen die niet willen dat de kerk afdwaalt, maar zij hebben hun eigen problemen—liefde voor geld, hebzucht en een liefhebben van plezier. Niemand zegt iets omdat het lijkt alsof niemand het wil horen. Een populaire reactie is: "Ja, ik weet dat het niet goed is, maar wat kunnen we doen?" "Alle kerken hebben problemen." Of: "Ja, ik zou dat nooit toestaan, maar ik voel niet dat het mijn plaats is om er iets van te zeggen." "Het is niet voor mijn gezin, maar als anderen dat willen doen, is het goed."

We leven in een "ik"-tijdperk. Alles draait om mij. De conservatieve, anabaptistische mensen raken verstrikt in sociale media, selfies, twitteren, Facebook en noem maar op. We houden zoveel van onszelf dat we praten, handelen en kleden op manieren die aandacht op ons vestigen—we promoten onszelf. We praten over er goed uitzien, je goed voelen en goed leven. Wat is er gebeurd met het promoten van Jezus? Denk eraan, Jezus zei: Want wie zijn leven wil behouden, zal het verliezen; maar wie zijn leven om mijn wil verliest, zal het vinden – Mattheüs 16:25.

Waarom lijkt het zo moeilijk te zijn te zeggen welke kant we opgaan? Als alles om onszelf draait, dan draait het niet om Jezus. Als we bezig zijn met de laatste mode en de mooiste auto’s, vrachtwagens en huizen, dan draait het niet om Jezus. We kunnen ons niet overgeven aan het plezieren van het vlees en toch zeggen dat we christenen zijn.

Onlangs werd mij gevraagd waarom sommige predikanten hun kinderen aan de wereld verliezen. In de meeste gevallen geloof ik dat het om dezelfde reden is dat veel Anabaptisten hun kinderen aan het koninkrijk van de duisternis verliezen—de vaders hebben een goddelijke visie voor hun huizen verloren. Ze leven een machteloos leven en laten de wereld binnenkomen. Misschien hebben ze geen televisie, maar wat met het internet? Dat laat nog steeds de invloed van de wereld binnenkomen. Ook besteedt vader meer tijd aan zijn bedrijf en meer tijd aan het genieten van het leven dan aan het zoeken naar het aangezicht van God.

Veel Amerikanen gaan op korte termijn zendingswerk. Vaak lijkt het alsof de jongeren die meegaan zo snel mogelijk het strand of een ander genoegen en ontspanning willen opzoeken zodra ze uit het vliegtuig stappen. Waarom? Omdat dat is wat hen thuis geleerd of toegestaan wordt—het zoeken van plezier. Ze zijn niet geleerd het vlees te verloochenen; ze hebben hun ouders het vlees niet zien verloochenen. Sommigen van ons zijn misschien zo ver van de koers af dat we moeten doen zoals de timmerman aan het begin van dit artikel—ons vernederen en opnieuw beginnen.

Mannen slepen hun tegenstrevende vrouwen de wereld in, vrouwen duwen hun mannen de wereld in, en kinderen slepen hun ouders de wereld in. En helaas, omdat de moderne kerk alle vormen van tucht en structuur heeft afgesmeten, kan iedereen in de kerk blijven en haar vervuilen met hun wereldse ideeën (althans zolang je lacht en zegt dat je van Jezus houdt). Denk aan de Schriften: Als gij Mij liefhebt, houdt dan Mijn geboden – Johannes 14:15. En: wie zegt: Ik ken Hem, en houdt Zijn geboden niet, die is een leugenaar, en in hem is de waarheid niet – 1 Johannes 2:4.

Hier zijn enkele gebieden van afglijden in de kerk.

Broederlijke liefde

Hieraan zullen allen weten dat gij Mijn discipelen zijt, indien gij liefde hebt onder elkander – Johannes 13:35.

Mensen hebben onze kerk bezocht en gevraagd of wij de heilige kus beoefenen. Ik antwoord dat wij dat doen; echter, het begrip van de noodzaak om elkaar lief te hebben komt eerst. Veel kerken schaffen de heilige kus af, wat duidelijk in het Woord wordt geboden. En het lijkt passend omdat zij zijn opgehouden elkaar lief te hebben. Ik geloof niet dat wij het belang van dit onderwerp—elkaar liefhebben—voldoende begrijpen. Wanneer onze liefde ons veroorzaakt voor elkaar te lijden, ziet de wereld het. Vaak houdt een broederschap op elkaar lief te hebben omdat zij niet meer samen in de strijd zijn. Ze zijn zelfstandig geworden.

Sommige van de grootste daden van liefde voor elkaar hebben plaatsgevonden op het slagveld. Mannen hebben zich voor granaatscherven geworpen en zich voor kogels geworpen om hun kameraden te redden. Omdat zij samen gevochten hebben, letten zij op elkaar. Wat als een soldaat die op mars gaat naar het gevecht zou zien dat de munitielade van een kameraad uit zijn geweer valt? Wat zou hij doen? Zou hij zwijgen omdat zijn kameraad misschien boos wordt? Of zou hij zwijgen omdat hij weet dat hij zijn eigen problemen heeft? Nee. Hij zou zijn broer helpen. Als onheilige mannen op het slagveld dit kunnen doen, waarom kunnen Gods mensen dat dan niet in de kerk? Voordat ik bekeerd werd, zat ik in het leger. Ik koos ervoor te lijden voor mijn land. Nu ik christen ben, kies ik ervoor te lijden voor mijn Heer.

Kleding

Dit is het meest voor de hand liggende, maar ook het meest over het hoofd geziene. De wereldse kerk zegt: "Het hart is wat telt, dus hoe we eruitzien van buiten maakt niets uit." Zijn de Anabaptisten hiervoor aan het vallen? De wereld kleedde zich vroeger bescheiden, maar televisie en Hollywood begonnen de focus op het menselijk lichaam te promoten. Zeker de kerk zou Hollywood niet volgen. Maar wat is het verschil—een vrouw van de wereld die duidelijk onkuis gekleed is, of een vrouw van de kerk gekleed in een cape-jurk die nauwsluitend is, en met een klein hoofdbedekkinkje dat schamel op de achterkant van haar hoofd hangt? Er is weinig verschil, behalve dat de een beweert christen te zijn en de ander niet. Lieve mensen, de wereld lacht ons uit.

Hoe begint het allemaal? Subtiel. Eerst verwijder je hier een plooi of daar een plissé, dan begin je wat minder stof te gebruiken, uiteindelijk koop je feller, opvallender kleuren. De mannen stoppen het overhemd uit de broek, schakelen over op jeans, daarna skinny jeans, maken een paar knopen los, laten hun haar iets groeien. Koopt een paar van die "coole" merk-schoenen en een cowboyhoed. De duivel is geen dwaas. Als je een kikker in kokend water gooit, springt hij er snel uit. Als je het water met de kikker erin langzaam aan de kook brengt, zal hij langzaam gaar gekookt worden. Is het te laat om eruit te springen? Met God is alle dingen mogelijk. Broeders en zusters, het is het hart dat telt; en als we verlangen eruit te zien als de wereld, is ons hart werelds en moet het gereinigd worden—gereinigd door het machtige bloed van Jezus.

Plezier

Gij hebt op aarde in weelde geleefd en zijt verslindende geweest; gij hebt uw hart gevoed op een dag des slachtens. Gij hebt het recht veroordeeld en gedood, en het verzet u niet – Jakobus 5:5-6.

Maar het dat tussen de doornen viel, dat zijn zij, die het gehoord hebbende, door de zorgen en de rijkdom en de begoochelingen van dit leven worden verstikt, en zij brengen geen vrucht tot volmaaktheid – Lukas 8:14.

En dit weet gij ook: dat er in de laatste dagen moeilijke tijden zullen komen. Want de mensen zullen eigenliefhebbers zijn, geldgierig, zelfverheffend, hoogmoedig, lasteraars, ongehoorzaam aan ouders, ondankbaar, onheilig, zonder natuurlijke liefde, vredesbrekers, lasteraars, onmatig, wreed, haters van het goede, verraders, overmoedig, hooghartig, liefhebbers van genoegens meer dan liefhebbers van God; terwijl zij een schijn van godzaligheid hebben, maar de kracht ervan verloochenen. Van solchen wendt u af – 2 Timoteüs 3:1-5.

Wanneer wij aan plezier toegeven, scheiden we onszelf af van de lijdensweg waarop wij geroepen zijn, en scheiden we ons dus af van de beloning die uit lijden voortkomt.

Denk eraan, wanneer wij een beetje toegeven in een kwestie in onze generatie, zullen onze kinderen er verder mee meegaan. Wanneer onze kinderen alleen van de kerk houden vanwege het volleybalspel dat erna gepland is, is dat niet goed. Wanneer ze op een zendingsreis heen willen vanwege de geneugten van de zee, is dat niet goed. Ik zeg niet dat die dingen slecht zijn, maar wanneer ze het middelpunt worden, hebben we een serieus probleem. Genieten we van de dingen die God behaagd? Genieten we nog van het zingen van hymnen? Genieten we ervan de armen te helpen? Wat dacht je van de weduwen bezoeken? Ik geloof dat als de vaders hun prioriteiten op orde hebben en zij werkelijk graag de dingen van God doen, zelfs als het vlees lijdt, dat dan ook onze kinderen (de volgende generatie) zo zullen doen, waarvoor WIJ verantwoordelijk zijn. Ik zeg vaak tegen mensen dat zij Jezus niet hoeven te volgen. Zij kunnen van de wereld houden en van de genoegens van dit leven, maar zij kunnen niet blijven zitten in onze kerk en doen alsof ze christenen zijn. Mensen zouden kunnen zeggen dat dat te hard is, maar ik geloof dat Jezus hetzelfde zei. Ik ken uw werken: gij zijt noch koud noch heet. Och, dat gij koud of heet waart! Zo omdat gij lauw zijt, noch koud noch heet, zal ik u uit mijn mond spuwen – Openbaring 3:15-16.

Dit is geen volledige lijst, want er zijn vele andere manieren waarop de kerk naar de wereld afdrijft. Mijn gebed is dat wij, ten eerste, het probleem kunnen zien, en ten tweede, dat wij het kunnen aanpakken. Gedenk: een beetje gist doet het hele deeg rijzen. (1 Korintiërs 5)

Er woedt een strijd; het koninkrijk der duisternis dringt aan. De duivel weet werkelijk dat hij maar weinig tijd heeft. Laten wij standhouden, onze witte vlaggen neerleggen en onze zwaarden oppakken. Laten wij de verraders, de wereld en de zonde die in de kerk is gekomen verwijderen. Laten wij de kerk zuiveren en de goede strijd des geloofs strijden.

Hoe stoppen we het afdrijven? Hoe laten we een getrouwe generatie achter? Eerst moeten de vaders hun kinderen onderwijzen, en de leiders in de kerk moeten hen allen onderwijzen. De vroege Anabaptisten kwamen zo vaak bijeen als ze maar konden, en dat was meestal in weer en wind, ergens in een bos. Onze kerk hier komt vijf keer per week samen. Alleen op zondag samenkomen, geloof ik, toont waar onze prioriteiten liggen.

En Hij heeft sommigen gegeven, apostelen; en sommigen, profeten; en sommigen, evangelisten; en sommigen, herders en leraars; tot de voleinding der heiligen, tot het werk van het ambt, tot de opbouw van het lichaam van Christus; Tot wij allen komen in de eenheid des geloofs en der kennis van de Zoon van God, tot een volwassen man, tot de maat der volheid van Christus – Efeziërs 4:11-13.

Het lijkt erop dat God ons leraren, herders, evangelisten, profeten en apostelen zou geven als wij ze zouden gebruiken.

Laten we het persoonlijk maken—er kunnen gebieden van afglijden in mijn leven zijn. We moeten elkaar helpen voordat we allen in verderf afdrijven. Misschien kunnen we standhouden, maar we moeten ook bezorgd zijn om onze kinderen. Als we bij elkaar konden komen en eerlijk konden zijn tegenover onszelf en tegenover elkaar over wat de Schriften duidelijk leren, zouden we voorzichtiger zijn. Als we Gods Woord samen met open hart en geest zouden bestuderen, geloof ik dat we datgene wat overblijft konden versterken. Ik geloof dat als wij op onze gezichten voor God zouden vallen, Hij onze kerken zou genezen. Moge God ons allen zegenen in een dieper wandel met Hem.

Freedom, or bondage—which will it be?
Or are they the same; can someone see?

People love things that money can buy,
They trade their lives, with no reason why.

The bills pile up for comforts and ease;
“What about our wives, or children to please?”

We spend all our days chasing the dollar.
The devil smiles as he tightens our collar.

We need time for God, and our families too.
Maybe less time at work could surely do.

Do we have time for that still small voice?
Or does our money talk, and give us no choice?

We all know the Bible—no work, no eat.
But money will bind us until death we meet.

The more we have, the more we need;
The love of money starts with a seed.

Lying to yourself is a foolish thing—
“Freedom, or bondage?” is the question I bring.

স্বাধীনতা, না দাসত্ব—কোনটি হবে?
না কি দুটোই কি এক; কে কি দেখবে?

মানুষ প্রেম করে সেই জিনিসে যা টাকা কিনতে পারে,
তারা বেচে দেয় তাদের জীবন, কেন—কারো জানা নেই।

আরাম আর স편তার জন্য বিল জমে যায়;
“আমাদের স্ত্রীরা বা সন্তানেরা কেমন হবে?” বলে চিন্তায় পড়ি।

ہمরা সব দিন কেবল ডলারের পিছু দৌড়াই।
শয়তান হাসে যখন সে আমাদের কলার টাইট করে।

আমাদের জন্য সময় দরকার ঈশ্বরেরও, আর পরিবারকেও।
হয়ত কাজের সময় কমালে তা নিশ্চয় সাহায্য করবে।

আমাদের কি সেই নীরব স্বরের জন্য সময় আছে?
না কি আমাদের টাকাই কথা বলে, আর কোনো নির্বাচন রাখে না?

আমরা সবাই বাইবেল জানি—কর্ম না করলে খাওয়া নেই।
কিন্তু টাকা আমাদের বেঁধে রাখে যতক্ষণ না মৃত্যু আসে।

যত বেশি পাই, তত বেশি দরকার মনে হয়;
টাকার প্রেম একটি বীজ থেকেই শুরু হয়।

নিজেকে মিথ্যা বলা একটি বোকা কাজ—
“স্বাধীনতা, না দাসত্ব?” এই প্রশ্ন আমি আনছি।

Jesus, upon His ascension back into His heavenly home, gave a final directive to His disciples, both to those physically present as He disappeared into the clouds, and to the myriad of believers who would come to know Him down through the ages. The story of His life and His gospel were to be preached unto all the world by those who called Him Lord. This global spreading of the Word, would, in the later vision of John, be proclaimed as one of the prerequisites of Jesus’ triumphant return at the end of time. John himself would be seen as a harbinger of these end times, based on Jesus’ words as recorded by John … If I will that he [John] tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. John 21:22.

The early Christians, understandably, felt that the return of Christ was imminent, even within the first century. The rapid expansion of Christianity, the complete moral depravity of the Roman culture, and the increasing intensity of persecution against them seemed to point to a swift and triumphant return of their Lord.

Now, two thousand years since Christ gave that promise, His soon return seems just as imminent as it did to the first century believers. Speculation on the time of His return, the manner of it, and the contributing factors are always current and controversial subjects. In the light of this continued earnest expectation of the end times, what have we to learn about our interpretations of prophecy from those who have attempted to decipher the prophetic portions of Scripture in earlier ages?

Jesus' first coming was surrounded and enveloped by perhaps the most recognizable misinterpretation of prophecy in the Bible. Roughly four hundred years of relative silence from God precluded His entry into the world in a physical, human body. His birth would be unnoticed in a society that was not only in desperate need of, but also expecting, a Savior to arrive. Daniel, writing the words God gave him, had told of a Messiah to come, and had even given a time that He would appear. Now, the Jews seethed under Roman rule, hanging their hopes on what they thought would be a sudden and triumphant extermination of the Roman troops and influence from their lands. To us, it is glaringly obvious that their interpretation of prophecy was not only incorrect, but for many, would lead them astray so that they did not even recognize or acknowledge the true Redeemer that was sent to them.

But what was it that caused this misinterpreted view? To us, it seems completely in order that Jesus would focus on the poor and destitute rather than opposing an occupying army. Jewish historians give an intriguing, but scarcely surprising, answer to the failure of the majority of their people to recognize Christ for who He was.

The religious atmosphere of first century Israel was one defined by corruption, bribery, lust for power, and all the unsavory aspects of a completely politically motivated upper class.

The priests, once chosen by God to be His servants in sanctifying His children, had sunk to buying their positions of service, most notably in the high priest’s office, where God had ordained one high priest to serve the people throughout his life. In Jesus’ day, however, the responsibilities of leading the children of Israel were divvied out, the role often changing hands on one-year terms. Becoming a high priest was a matter of birth. Most high priests came from several large, influential, and wealthy families, as one often had to buy into the opportunity of this office.

It was not only the high priest’s office that was corrupted, but most levels of prominent spiritual leadership were filled by the wealthy elites who had the connections and wealth to be placed into roles of importance amongst the Jews.

This unsavory backdrop gives even more clarity to Jesus’ feelings on the religious leaders of His day. These imposters did not hold their priestly positions to serve His Father, they held them for their own gain, turning the temple into a marketplace and holding the common people hostage through their disputes on the minutiae of the Law.

Unsurprisingly, these leaders looked for a Messiah who would fit their goals, their ideals, and their morals, rather than one that would rebuke and chastise them for their hypocrisy, greed, and selfish ambition. Their view of prophecy had been so twisted and corrupted by their lifestyle that even the miracle of a resurrection could not sway them to view Christ’s power as coming from God. This misconstrued expectation of a conquering commander, riding a horse of war over the political enemies of these elites was pandered to the common Jew as well. Centuries of fighting for just the freedom to worship, as in the case of the Maccabees and the Greeks, had deeply imprinted a sense of nationalism into the collective mind of the Jewish people. The ones who bought into it the most were the ones who received the most from this system of exclusive access to God and His promises. To those who were repressed by the stringent and often man-made laws of Jewish society, a God of peace and love who would draw the needy of the world to Him was more welcome than a Saviour who would simply install another earthly government to rule the poor, oppress the widows, and reward the wicked.

This was not the last time an oppressed people would be deceived, as Roman rule would witness another major misstep in the collective interpretations of God’s people. This time, the teachings of Jesus and the words of His disciples would be misinterpreted to fit the changing political and religious landscape of fourth century Rome. The year was 306, and Diocletian, one of the most brutal persecutors of Christians in the Roman Empire, had abdicated from his position as Caesar. In his wake, he left three contenders for his throne. One of those vying for the seat of power was a young general, experienced in politics, and power hungry. His name was Constantine, son of a prominent Roman officer and a lowly Greek Christian, Helena.

From his youth, Constantine followed in his father’s footsteps, fighting throughout the empire, rising to a rank of general. Now, on campaign in Britain, he turned his eyes to the ultimate prize of a Roman politico, the title of Caesar, and the seat of the emperor.

Constantine’s line to the throne was through his father. Diocletian had, during his rule, appointed additional Caesars to aid in ruling the empire. Constantine’s father was one of these, and despite being simply appointed to the position, it was expected that his status as a Caesar would pass to his son. Matters were not as simple as a mere transfer of titles, however.

Constantine’s rise was bloody, but his grip on power was set, until he remained the sole contender for the throne. The stage was set. He quickly undid the harsh decrees of Diocletian, legalizing Christianity and removing the persecution that had leveled churches, scattered families, and hunted down bishops and other church leadership. Almost overnight, a peace previously unheard of was gifted to these hounded believers.

The changes that Constantine made did not end, however, with merely legalizing Christianity. His sympathies ran deeper, and he made further moves to legitimize it as not only an accepted religion, but as the state religion.

To Christians eager for the return of Christ, this seemed almost unbelievable. In the span of a few short years the government had gone from crucifying, beheading, and torturing them to holding them up as examples to the rest of the empire. The favor seems to have affected the clarity with which they viewed the apparent reconciliation of the world to the church. Not only would they accept a position of power in the empire, but they would also accept Constantine as a benefactor and protector of the church itself. In their minds, the day of the Lord was come, and Constantine was the rod of iron with which God would rule.

And rule he did. The course of the church was soon swayed by this new and outside influence. Constantine sat in on meetings of the bishops, even though at the time he was not baptized nor was he even seeking baptism. The church’s new position as a tool of the state brought schisms, in-fighting, and contention at every turn. There remained a remnant, but most of the church would fall under the sway of a man motivated by a hunger for power, wealth, and influence.

Constantine would be baptized before his death, lending him even further credibility in the eyes of a straying church. Now separated from its original identity as sheep in this world, the coming centuries would see “Christians” become ravening wolves, destroying, killing, and corrupting.

In a matter more recently related to us as Anabaptists, the tale of the infamous Muensterites gives us a further example of the perils of misinterpreting prophecy, especially the prophecy regarding the second coming of Christ.

One of the great disadvantages of a heavily persecuted group is a tendency to lack stability, as evidenced by the varying beliefs developed by Anabaptist groups of the movement's first fifty years. Persecution would deprive a congregation of their leaders, who were often those most targeted by the authorities. A missing elder meant less teaching, which in turn led to more difficulty in guidance, and corrective doctrine. Even the most sincere and interconnected groups could fall into errors developed because of the lack of leadership to bring Biblical clarity and balance the brotherhood.

The situation in the Netherlands was of a rather volatile strain approaching the 1530s. Throughout the country, the Catholic Church remained the predominant religion, clinging to their power through ruthless displays of physical force, most often directed towards the minority Protestant congregations. This focus on quelling the Protestant influence was momentarily successful in this instance, with most of their groups dissolving and reintegrating into the Catholic Church or other groups.

One of the groups that was on the receiving end of this minor diaspora was the fledging Dutch Anabaptist church. For those Protestants who still refused to join the Catholics, the Anabaptists often became their choice of church, rapidly swelling their ranks. This had a profound effect on the local strain of Anabaptism, which without a doubt was fervent, but quite prone to chaos and upheaval.

By 1534 the tensions of this influx of new believers reached a breaking point, and the Anabaptist church of the Netherlands split into two main factions. The first, led by the two Philips brothers, Dirk and Obbe, adhered to the New Testament teachings of separation from church and state, as well as nonresistance. This would be the church of Menno Simmons, and the root of the Mennonite churches of today.

The other faction held to more radical beliefs, led by Jan Matthysz and Jan of Leiden. These two men became increasingly fanatical in their views of Christ’s return, believing that they would be central figures, instrumental in a kingdom that God would set up on Earth.

At the same time, social unrest was brewing, and spilled over in the city of Munster, located in northwest Germany, where the common people rose up, overthrowing their city’s government and expelling their Catholic bishop. The two Jans were quick to act, contacting the new leaders of the city, and eventually winning them over to their views.

The Jans moved to Munser in early 1534, and began sending out prophets and messengers, who called all “Anabaptists” to congregate at this “New Jerusalem”. The unrest of the area made their message all the more appealing, and thousands streamed into the city, intent in being part of this apocalyptic return of Christ.

There was, in fact, an apocalyptic return on the horizon, but not a return of Christ. This one came in the form of the ousted Catholic bishop, who swiftly set siege to the city. His army would stay there for eighteen months.

Inside the city, Jan Matthysz, proclaiming a vision was given to him for a deliverance of the city, left its walls to parade outside, proclaiming a swift delivery of the enemy into his hands. His vision, however, failed him, as he was swiftly delivered into the hands of the enemy, where he was beheaded, and his head set on a pike in front Munster’s gates.

Inside the walls, Jan of Leiden took leadership, ignoring the famine, death, and chaos that now ran rampant within the besieged walls. Instead, he began promoting polygamy, defending it from the Old Testament, killing at least one woman who refused to marry him, and at one point, having sixteen wives.

This abomination soon led to its required end as the city was overcome, with a heavy slaughter being carried out against its inhabitants. The leaders, Jan of Leiden being the most prominent, were captured, tortured, and killed. Their bodies were hung in iron cages on the tower of St. Lamberts Church, the Catholic church in Munster. To this day, the cages still hang, a bleak reminder of the pride and rashness of the two Jans, determined to see their end-time interpretation fulfilled.

In all three of these examples, the prophecy contained in God’s Word was twisted into results that strayed far from the will of God for His children. For the Jews, it caused them to miss the Messiah, failing to recognize the greatest promise God had given them. The fourth century Christians, chafing under the horrific persecution of Diocletian, accepted Constantine as a deliverer, seeing him as a fulfillment of God’s judgement against the kingdoms of this world. Instead of peace, they would sink into a state of ungodliness worse than the pagans around them, with the Catholic Church straying into sin more horrible than even their pagan society. Lastly, the troubled visions and interpretations of the 16th century Munsterites would lead them to an awful fate, sullying the name of the true church.

What have we to learn from these grave errors of those before us? In our time, the end seems imminent, and we are beset with those who would have us believe that we are truly the last of the Christians.

Luke has recorded the instructions of Jesus on this point: …The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see it. And they shall say to you, See here; or, see there: go not after them, nor follow them –Luke 17: 22-23. Here are instructions for our conduct in the last days. Let us not be running after the rumors of the end times but let us be obedient to the final admonition of our Lord—that we spread the Word of God and the Gospel of His Son, Jesus throughout the world … and then shall the end come –Matthew 24:14.

Gesù, alla sua ascensione nel suo dimora celeste, diede un ultimo comandamento ai suoi discepoli, sia a quelli fisicamente presenti mentre scompariva tra le nuvole, sia alla moltitudine di credenti che Lo avrebbero conosciuto nei secoli a venire. La storia della sua vita e il suo vangelo dovevano essere predicati a tutto il mondo da coloro che Lo chiamavano Signore. Questa diffusione globale della Parola, sarebbe stata, nella visione finale di Giovanni, proclamata come uno dei prerequisiti del trionfante ritorno di Gesù alla fine dei tempi. Giovanni stesso sarebbe stato visto come un araldo di questi tempi ultimi, basato sulle parole di Gesù così come registrate da Giovanni … If I will that he [John] tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. John 21:22.

I primi cristiani, comprensibilmente, sentirono che il ritorno di Cristo fosse imminente, perfino nel primo secolo. La rapida espansione del cristianesimo, la completa depravazione morale della cultura romana e l'intensificarsi delle persecuzioni contro di loro sembravano indicare un rapido e trionfante ritorno del loro Signore.

Ora, duemila anni dopo che Cristo diede quella promessa, il suo prossimo ritorno sembra altrettanto imminente come lo era per i credenti del primo secolo. Le speculazioni sul tempo del suo ritorno, sulla maniera con cui avverrà e sui fattori che vi contribuiscono sono sempre argomenti attuali e controversi. Alla luce di questa continua e fervente attesa dei tempi ultimi, cosa possiamo imparare sulle nostre interpretazioni delle profezie da coloro che hanno tentato di decifrare le parti profetiche delle Scritture in epoche precedenti?

La prima venuta di Gesù fu circondata e avvolta da forse la più riconoscibile errata interpretazione di profezia nella Bibbia. Circa quattrocento anni di relativo silenzio da parte di Dio precedettero il suo ingresso nel mondo in un corpo fisico e umano. La sua nascita sarebbe passata inosservata in una società che non solo aveva disperato bisogno, ma anche aspettava un Salvatore. Daniele, scrivendo le parole che Dio gli aveva dato, aveva parlato di un Messia a venire, e aveva anche indicato un tempo in cui sarebbe apparso. Ora, gli Ebrei ribollivano sotto il dominio romano, riponendo le loro speranze in ciò che pensavano sarebbe stata una improvvisa e trionfante sconfitta delle truppe e dell'influenza romane dalle loro terre. Per noi è lampante che la loro interpretazione della profezia non era solo errata, ma per molti li avrebbe sviati tanto da non riconoscere né riconoscere il vero Redentore che era stato inviato loro.

Ma che cosa causò questa visione erronea? A noi sembra del tutto comprensibile che Gesù si concentrasse sui poveri e sui bisognosi anziché opporsi a un esercito occupante. Gli storici ebrei forniscono una risposta interessante, ma poco sorprendente, al fallimento della maggior parte del loro popolo nel riconoscere Cristo per quello che era.

L'atmosfera religiosa della Israele del primo secolo era definita da corruzione, tangenti, brama di potere e tutti gli aspetti sgradevoli di un'alta classe totalmente motivata politicamente.

I sacerdoti, una volta scelti da Dio per essere i suoi servitori nel santificare i suoi figli, erano scesi a comprare le loro posizioni di servizio, più notoriamente nell'ufficio del sommo sacerdote, dove Dio aveva ordinato che un sommo sacerdote servisse il popolo per tutta la vita. Ai tempi di Gesù, però, le responsabilità di guidare il popolo d'Israele venivano suddivise, il ruolo spesso cambiando di mano su basi annuali. Diventare sommo sacerdote era una questione di nascita. La maggior parte dei sommi sacerdoti provenivano da alcune grandi famiglie influenti e ricche, poiché spesso bisognava comprare l'opportunità di accedere a quell'ufficio.

Non era solo l'ufficio del sommo sacerdote a essere corrotto, ma la maggior parte dei livelli di leadership spirituale prominente era occupata dalle élite benestanti che avevano le conoscenze e la ricchezza per essere collocate in ruoli di importanza tra gli Ebrei.

Questo sfondo sgradevole chiarisce ancora di più i sentimenti di Gesù nei confronti dei capi religiosi del suo tempo. Questi impostori non mantenevano le loro posizioni sacerdotali per servire il suo Padre, le detenevano per il proprio guadagno, trasformando il tempio in un mercato e tenendo il popolo comune in ostaggio tramite le loro dispute sulle minuzie della Legge.

Non sorprende che questi leader cercassero un Messia che si adattasse ai loro scopi, ai loro ideali e alla loro morale, piuttosto che uno che li rimproverasse e castigasse per la loro ipocrisia, avidità e ambizione egoistica. La loro visione della profezia era stata così distorta e corrotta dal loro stile di vita che persino il miracolo di una risurrezione non li convinse a vedere il potere di Cristo come proveniente da Dio. Questa aspettativa equivocata di un comandante conquistatore, che cavalcava un cavallo da guerra sopra i nemici politici di queste élite, veniva blandita anche al Giudeo comune. Secoli di lotte per la sola libertà di culto, come nel caso dei Maccabei contro i Greci, avevano impresso profondamente un senso di nazionalismo nella coscienza collettiva del popolo ebraico. Coloro che più vi avevano aderito erano quelli che ricevevano di più da questo sistema di accesso esclusivo a Dio e alle sue promesse. Per gli oppressi dalle leggi stringenti e spesso fatte dall'uomo della società ebraica, un Dio di pace e amore che avrebbe attratto a sé i bisognosi del mondo era più gradito di un Salvatore che si limitasse a istituire un altro governo terreno per governare i poveri, opprimere le vedove e premiare gli empi.

Questa non fu l'ultima volta che un popolo oppresso sarebbe stato ingannato, poiché il dominio romano assisterà a un altro grande passo falso nelle interpretazioni collettive del popolo di Dio. Questa volta, gli insegnamenti di Gesù e le parole dei suoi discepoli sarebbero stati fraintesi per adattarsi al mutato panorama politico e religioso della Roma del IV secolo. L'anno era il 306, e Diocleziano, uno dei persecutori più brutali dei cristiani nell'Impero Romano, aveva abdicato dalla sua posizione di Cesare. Alle sue spalle lasciò tre contendenti per il trono. Uno di quelli che aspiravano al potere era un giovane generale, con esperienza politica e assetato di potere. Si chiamava Costantino, figlio di un ufficiale romano di rilievo e di un'umile cristiana greca, Elena.

Sin dalla giovinezza, Costantino seguì le orme di suo padre, combattendo in tutto l'impero e salendo al grado di generale. Ora, in campagna in Britannia, rivolse lo sguardo al premio supremo di un politico romano, il titolo di Cesare e la sede dell'imperatore.

La linea di successione di Costantino al trono passava attraverso suo padre. Diocleziano aveva, durante il suo governo, nominato Cesari aggiuntivi per aiutare nel governo dell'impero. Il padre di Costantino era uno di questi, e nonostante fosse stato semplicemente nominato alla posizione, si prevedeva che il suo status di Cesare passasse al figlio. Le cose non furono però così semplici come un mero trasferimento di titoli.

La salita di Costantino fu sanguinosa, ma la sua presa sul potere si consolidò, finché non rimase l'unico contendente al trono. La scena era pronta. Egli annullò rapidamente i decreti rigidi di Diocleziano, legalizzando il cristianesimo e rimuovendo le persecuzioni che avevano raso al suolo chiese, disperso famiglie e dato la caccia a vescovi e ad altri leader della chiesa. Quasi da un giorno all'altro, fu donata a questi credenti perseguitati una pace fino ad allora inedita.

I cambiamenti introdotti da Costantino non si limitarono però a legalizzare il cristianesimo. Le sue simpatie erano più profonde e fece ulteriori mosse per legittimarlo non solo come religione accettata, ma come religione di stato.

Per i cristiani ansiosi del ritorno di Cristo, ciò sembrò quasi incredibile. Nel giro di pochi anni il governo era passato dal crocifiggerli, decapitarli e torturarli, al presentarli come esempi per il resto dell'impero. Il favore sembrò influire sulla chiarezza con cui vedevano la apparente riconciliazione del mondo con la chiesa. Non solo accettarono una posizione di potere nell'impero, ma accolsero anche Costantino come benefattore e protettore della chiesa stessa. Nelle loro menti, il giorno del Signore era giunto, e Costantino era la verga di ferro con cui Dio avrebbe governato.

E governò davvero. Il corso della chiesa fu presto condizionato da questa nuova influenza esterna. Costantino prese parte alle riunioni dei vescovi, anche se all'epoca non era battezzato né stava cercando il battesimo. La nuova posizione della chiesa come strumento dello stato portò scismi, lotte interne e contesa a ogni passo. Rimase un rimanente, ma la maggior parte della chiesa cadde sotto l'influsso di un uomo mosso da fame di potere, ricchezza e influenza.

Costantino fu battezzato prima della sua morte, conferendogli ancora maggiore credibilità agli occhi di una chiesa smarrita. Ora separata dalla sua identità originaria come pecore in questo mondo, i secoli a venire avrebbero visto i “cristiani” diventare lupi famelici, distruggendo, uccidendo e corrompendo.

In un episodio più recente a noi riferito come anabattista, il racconto degli infami Münsteriti ci offre un ulteriore esempio dei pericoli di una errata interpretazione della profezia, specialmente della profezia riguardante la seconda venuta di Cristo.

Uno dei grandi svantaggi di un gruppo fortemente perseguitato è la tendenza a mancare di stabilità, come dimostrano le credenze variabili sviluppate dai gruppi anabattisti nei primi cinquant'anni del movimento. La persecuzione privava una congregazione dei suoi leader, spesso i più presi di mira dalle autorità. Un anziano mancato significava meno insegnamento, il che a sua volta portava a maggiori difficoltà nella guida e nella dottrina correttiva. Anche i gruppi più sinceri e interconnessi potevano cadere in errori sviluppati per la mancanza di leadership che portasse chiarezza biblica e equilibrio nella fratellanza.

La situazione nei Paesi Bassi era piuttosto volatile verso gli anni 1530. In tutto il paese, la Chiesa cattolica rimaneva la religione predominante, aggrappandosi al proprio potere tramite display spietati di forza fisica, spesso diretti contro le congregazioni protestanti minoritarie. Questo sforzo per sedare l'influenza protestante ebbe un successo momentaneo in questo caso, con la maggior parte dei loro gruppi che si sciolsero e si reintegrarono nella Chiesa cattolica o in altri gruppi.

Uno dei gruppi che si trovò a beneficiare di questa minore diaspora fu la nascente chiesa anabattista olandese. Per quei protestanti che ancora rifiutavano di unirsi ai cattolici, gli anabattisti divennero spesso la loro scelta di chiesa, facendo rapidamente aumentare il loro numero. Questo ebbe un profondo effetto sul ceppo locale di anabattismo, che senza dubbio era fervente, ma piuttosto incline al caos e ai rivolgimenti.

Entro il 1534, le tensioni causate da questo afflusso di nuovi credenti raggiunsero un punto di rottura e la chiesa anabattista dei Paesi Bassi si divise in due principali fazioni. La prima, guidata dai due fratelli Philips, Dirk e Obbe, aderiva agli insegnamenti del Nuovo Testamento sulla separazione tra chiesa e stato, nonché sulla non resistenza. Questa sarebbe stata la chiesa di Menno Simons e la radice delle chiese mennonite odierne.

L'altra fazione sosteneva credenze più radicali, guidata da Jan Matthysz e Jan di Leida. Questi due uomini divennero sempre più fanatici nelle loro vedute del ritorno di Cristo, credendo che sarebbero stati figure centrali, strumentali in un regno che Dio avrebbe stabilito sulla terra.

Allo stesso tempo, fermenti di malcontento sociale stavano covando e sfociarono nella città di Münster, situata nel nord-ovest della Germania, dove il popolo comune si sollevò, rovesciando il governo della città ed espellendo il loro vescovo cattolico. I due Jan agirono rapidamente, contattarono i nuovi leader della città e alla fine li convinsero delle loro vedute.

I Jan si trasferirono a Münster all'inizio del 1534 e cominciarono a inviare profeti e messaggeri, che chiamavano tutti gli “anabattisti” a radunarsi in questa “Nuova Gerusalemme”. L'agitazione dell'area rese il loro messaggio ancor più allettante e migliaia confluirono nella città, intenzionati a far parte di questo apocalittico ritorno di Cristo.

In effetti, c'era un ritorno apocalittico all'orizzonte, ma non era il ritorno di Cristo. Questo arrivò sotto forma del vescovo cattolico spodestato, che rapidamente mise la città sotto assedio. Il suo esercito vi rimase per diciotto mesi.

All'interno della città, Jan Matthysz, proclamando di aver ricevuto una visione per la liberazione della città, lasciò le mura per sfilare all'esterno, proclamando una rapida consegna del nemico nelle sue mani. La sua visione, tuttavia, lo abbandonò, poiché egli fu consegnato alle mani del nemico, dove fu decollato e la sua testa posta su un palo davanti alle porte di Münster.

Dentro le mura, Jan di Leida prese il comando, ignorando la carestia, la morte e il caos che ormai imperversavano all'interno delle mura assediate. Invece, iniziò a promuovere la poligamia, difendendola dall'Antico Testamento, uccidendo almeno una donna che rifiutò di sposarlo e, in un certo periodo, avendo sedici mogli.

Questa abominazione portò presto al suo necessario epilogo quando la città fu conquistata, con un massacro pesante inflitto ai suoi abitanti. I leader, Jan di Leida essendo il più prominente, furono catturati, torturati e uccisi. I loro corpi furono appesi in gabbie di ferro sulla torre della chiesa di San Lamberto, la chiesa cattolica di Münster. Ancora oggi le gabbie pendono, un cupo monito dell'orgoglio e della precipitazione dei due Jan, determinati a vedere la loro interpretazione dei tempi ultimi adempiuta.

In tutti e tre questi esempi, la profezia contenuta nella Parola di Dio fu distorta in risultati che si allontanarono di molto dalla volontà di Dio per i suoi figli. Per gli Ebrei, ciò causò il mancato riconoscimento del Messia, fallendo nel riconoscere la più grande promessa che Dio aveva dato loro. I cristiani del quarto secolo, strozzati dalla terribile persecuzione di Diocleziano, accettarono Costantino come un liberatore, vedendolo come un adempimento del giudizio di Dio contro i regni di questo mondo. Invece della pace, sarebbero precipitati in uno stato di empietà peggiore dei pagani che li circondavano, con la Chiesa cattolica che si smarrì in peccati più orribili persino della loro società pagana. Infine, le visioni travagliate e le interpretazioni dei münsteriti del XVI secolo li condussero a un destino terribile, macchiando il nome della vera chiesa.

Cosa dobbiamo apprendere da questi gravi errori di coloro che ci hanno preceduto? Ai nostri tempi, la fine sembra imminente e siamo assaliti da coloro che vorrebbero farci credere che siamo davvero gli ultimi dei cristiani.

Luca ha registrato le istruzioni di Gesù su questo punto: …The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see it. And they shall say to you, See here; or, see there: go not after them, nor follow them –Luke 17: 22-23. Qui ci sono istruzioni per il nostro comportamento negli ultimi giorni. Non inseguiamo i pettegolezzi sui tempi ultimi, ma siamo obbedienti all'ultima ammonizione del nostro Signore—che diffondiamo la Parola di Dio e il Vangelo del suo Figlio, Gesù, in tutto il mondo … and then shall the end come –Matthew 24:14.

Freedom, or bondage—which will it be?
Or are they the same; can someone see?

People love things that money can buy,
They trade their lives, with no reason why.

The bills pile up for comforts and ease;
“What about our wives, or children to please?”

We spend all our days chasing the dollar.
The devil smiles as he tightens our collar.

We need time for God, and our families too.
Maybe less time at work could surely do.

Do we have time for that still small voice?
Or does our money talk, and give us no choice?

We all know the Bible—no work, no eat.
But money will bind us until death we meet.

The more we have, the more we need;
The love of money starts with a seed.

Lying to yourself is a foolish thing—
“Freedom, or bondage?” is the question I bring.

This story starts in Switzerland, in the 1500s. A group of Christian believers, desiring to obey Jesus and return to the teachings of the Apostles and the early Church, separated from both the Catholic and Protestant state-run Churches in several Cantons of Switzerland. They were referred to as the Swiss Brethren and were deemed as enemies of the state, by the Catholics and Protestants alike. Their enemies called them “Anabaptists” because they rejected infant baptism. They also refused military service, obeying Christ’s commands to “bless them that persecute you” and “love your enemies”. Many were arrested, imprisoned, tortured mercilessly and finally, many were martyred for not recanting their faith. In the early 1600s, when the authorities could not stop the movement in this manner, they began confiscating the believer’s homes, farms, and belongings, then exiled them from Switzerland.

Europe had just gone through the devastations of the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648). In some places, like the Palatinate (Pfaltzland) in Germany, as many as 70% of the inhabitants had died of either war or disease. Many of the Hoffs (house/barn fort enclosures) were burned out and the fields were left uncultivated for years. In the mid-1600s, the local Prince, Elector Ludwig, invited the exiled Swiss Brethren into the Palatinate to help rebuild the farms because of their reputation as excellent husbandmen and tillers of the soil.

There were three official Churches recognized by the Germans: Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed. Although the Swiss Brethren were needed economically, and their faith was tolerated, their churches were not recognized. There were limits on how many of them could meet together at one time, and many times they were not allowed to purchase the farms that they were improving because they were considered foreigners.

The Swiss-operated farms did indeed prosper in time, partly due to their use of a superior crop rotation system, which helped them feed more dairy cattle, and, in turn, allowed them to produce milk through the winters. Another major improvement was the introduction of the legume, clover. This came from seed which the Dutch Mennonites gifted to them. After about 50 years, the difference the Swiss had made in agriculture was noticeable enough that some frustrated German neighbors accused them of “Ferhexing” (the Pennsylvania Dutch term for witchcraft) the ground (which of course was not true). So, life in the Pfaltzland wasn’t getting better for the Swiss Brethren.

In the year 1708, they experienced a bitterly cold, long winter. So cold that some of their stored root crops froze in the cold cellars. Sometime after this, William Penn and the Quakers heard of the plight of these Swiss Anabaptists. In 1682, William Penn had been granted the colony of Pennsylvania and wanted to conduct what he called the “Holy Experiment”. He envisioned a land where all races and religions could dwell together in peace. He had special interest in those groups persecuted by the European State Churches. As a Quaker, he too had suffered persecution by the state church of England. He welcomed Quakers from England, Huguenots from France, Mennonites from Holland, German Baptist, Schwenkfelders and Pietists from Germany, as well as Swiss Brethren and Jews from wherever they were sojourning and/or suffering.

That is the background for our account of Hans Graeff (Groff) who lived from c.1661-1746. Hans had been converted to the faith of the Swiss Brethren, but his wife, Anna (Bare) Graeff had stayed with the Protestant State Church. When the door opened to pioneer in Pennsylvania, Hans was interested in going, but Anna was not. Possibly they planned to have him get settled in over there and then come back for her. Hans first came to Pennsylvania in 1696. Later, Hans ended up leading a small group of the Swiss Brethren (Hans & Christian Herr, Martin Meylin, Jacob Muller, Martin Kendig, Martin Oberholtzer, Wendell Bowman & the Funks to name a few) to Germantown, about seven miles north of Philadelphia in that day, which was the first permanent settlement of the Anabaptists in the New World. Many of those first settlers were from Holland and Sweden and were part of the Mennonite Church of the Netherlands. The Swiss immigrants spent the winter of 1709 in Germantown—the women doing spinning for the many weavers of Germantown and the men traveling to a new Anabaptist settlement at Skippack, where they were learning many of the skills needed to go to the frontier. It seems that here is where the Swiss Brethren first became known as Mennists or Mennonites.

In 1710, the group moved up to the Conestoga Valley where Hans Groff had previously identified some very rich and well-watered lands, 60 miles west of Germantown and civilization. Life would indeed be difficult. Wolves, bears, panthers, bobcats and other predators abounded. There were also elk, timber bison, and whitetail deer in abundance (which were glad to eat whatever the settlers planted). Huge walnut, hickory, chestnuts, maples, white pines, and oaks, some six feet in diameter and over 100 feet tall, covered much of their new lands (except for some open meadows, left by the native Americans and wetlands). These huge trees would need to be cut down by hand with axes and two-man saws. The closest doctor, apothecary, hardware, or general store was 60 miles away. It would be challenging and dangerous work, but they were free! Free to obey their conscience. Free to practice their religion. Free to own land in this beautiful wilderness. Free to love and witness to their neighbors—the Conestoga tribe and French traders. They received a land patent for 10,000 acres for their families and others that might come later.

Partly due to severe persecution, in 1710, a group of Swiss Brethren moved to the Mannheim area of Germany. Seven years later, in 1717, they made the trip across the Atlantic. There were more than 60 families that came to the Conestoga Valley in the fall of that year, including my ancestors, Hans and Magdalena Hess and their three children (they were eventually blessed with a total of 11). You could say that from then on, the floodgates opened, and masses of Anabaptists fled Europe to “Penn’s Promised Land”. From 1730 and later, as this wilderness became tamed, there were also many Lutheran, Reformed, and Catholic people who came over from Germany to find better financial opportunities, filling this part of Pennsylvania with many German-dialect speakers.

I greatly enjoyed speaking with the noted Lancaster County Anabaptist historian, Amos Hoover, while writing this article. He gave many insights and details, but we both agreed, it is challenging to put together all the facts and details from so long ago. Gleaning from a couple authors’ accounts, the story goes something like this:

Misunderstanding

Sometime, after being in Penn’s woods for a number of years, Hans Groff received word that his wife, Anna (Bare) Groff, back in Europe, had passed away. He was very grieved and mourned, as he didn’t know it and wasn’t there to bury her. In a few years, he married Susanna Kendig. They lived first in the Strasburg area, then built a substantial homestead in the area now called Groffdale. This union was blessed with nine children.

Years later, a woman showed up in the community and introduced herself as Mrs. Hans Groff. She had become an Anabaptist in Europe and had made the perilous trip across the Atlantic to find her husband. According to her, a person with the same name as herself had died, and the word given to Hans was not true about his first wife’s death. Hans was mortified, although he was innocent regarding his second marriage. He had no desire to be a polygamist or to commit adultery. The frontier church leaders held counsel and gave a recommendation—that the younger, pioneer wife with so many young children needed the husband to provide for them. It is said that Hans didn’t feel clear to stay with either of them but did support both of his wives and their children financially. He was noted as a tireless traveler, riding to Philadelphia with furs then back out into the vast frontier with blankets, brass kettles and other trade good for the Native Americans. If you have heard or read this account with different details, so have I. Only eternity will reveal all these details exactly.

Medicine

Hans’s first wife chose to live as a single sister in that church community. Instead of becoming bitter with her husband, her God, and her circumstances, she chose a life of service to her neighbors. She lived in a little house, with a small barn (possibly built by Hans for her) on top of a steep hill overlooking Farmersville, called “Cat’s Back Hill”. The ruins of this early 1700s house and barn were still evident less than 50 years ago. Apparently, she was a midwife, before coming to this country and continued in this profession once she was here. She had a lot of experience with growing herbs and making herbal remedies. She was possibly the closest one to being a doctor for many miles around. From what I can find out, she spent her time being a blessing to the local community with her medical knowledge and wisdom, her homemade herbal medicines, and her midwifery. Many of our Lancaster County forefathers may not have survived the rigorous pioneer life if it had not been for this dear Sister’s servanthood and medical knowledge. Interestingly, years later, one of Hans’s sons from the second wife, David Groff, went away to study medicine. Once his studies were completed, he came back as a doctor and helped his father’s first wife minister to the many settlers in fast growing Lancaster County.

This story provides a glimpse into some of the interesting details surrounding the life of conservative Anabaptists just before and during the establishing of Colonial America. There were difficulties involving freedom of religion and worship in their homelands of Europe, but their travels to, and eventual day-to-day living in, a new, free country was acquainted with challenges as well. One encouragement that we can see in this story was the willingness of these individuals to allow God’s principles to guide them each step of the way.
