I watched as a man attempted to cut a large sheet of plywood in half. He was talking with a few other men while he was cutting, and it seemed that he wasn’t too concerned about making the cut straight. I noticed that he continued to cut further and further from the line that he had scratched into the piece of plywood with a nail. After he was several inches off, one of his friends tried to point it out but he pretended to ignore him. He tried to casually guide the old handsaw back towards the line, while continuing to talk with the men, not making a big deal of it. Finally, after he was more than a foot off, he stopped. He knew now that he had a problem, a problem he could not fix.

I had to think, “Is this what we are doing as the church, the bride of Christ?” We are not too serious about drifting off the straight and narrow way; we allow things to come into our midst. We say, “It’s not a big deal, let’s not be critical.” But the longer we wait, the harder it will be to straighten out. At first it shocks us; later it becomes the new normal. How do we tell if we have drifted? It should be as easy as considering where we used to be, and comparing it that with where we are now, then evaluating the change with what the Bible teaches.

Since fighting against drift is not popular, men in the church don’t want to do it. Some people in our churches who are drifting towards the world have perfected a feel-good gospel. They go on and on about how close they are getting to Jesus, and how blessed they are, but their direction is clearly not in line with the teachings of Scripture. They’re headed towards the world.

There are others who don’t want the church to drift, yet they have their own problems—the love of money, covetousness, and a love of pleasure. No one says anything because it seems that nobody wants to hear. A popular response is, “Yes, I know it’s not good, but what can we do?” “All churches have problems.” Or “Yes, I would never allow that, but I don’t feel it’s in my place to speak up about it.” “It’s not for my family, but if others want to do that, its fine.”

We live in a “me” age. Everything is about me. The conservative, Anabaptist people are getting tangled up in social media, selfies, tweeting, Facebook, and you name it. We love ourselves to the extent that we talk, act, and dress in ways that draw attention to ourselves—we promote ourselves. We talk about looking good, feeling good, and living good. What happened to promoting Jesus? Remember, Jesus said: For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it –Matthew 16:25.

Why does it seem so hard to tell which direction we are going? If we are all about ourselves, then we are not all about Jesus. If we are into the latest fashions and the nicest cars, trucks, and houses, then we are not all about Jesus. We cannot indulge ourselves in pleasing the flesh, and still say we are Christians.

I was recently asked why some pastors lose their children to the world. In most cases, I believe it’s the same reason that many Anabaptists are losing their children to the kingdom of darkness—the fathers have lost a godly vision for their homes. They live a powerless life and allow the world to come in. Maybe they do not have television, but what about the internet? This still allows the influence of the world to come in. Also, Dad spends more time with his business and more time enjoying life than he does seeking the face of God.

Many Americans go on short-term missions. Many times, it seems that the youth who go want to hit the beach or some other pleasure and relaxation as soon as they get off the plane. Why? Because that’s what they are either taught or allowed to do back home—seek pleasure. They haven’t been taught to deny the flesh; they haven’t seen their parents deny the flesh. Some of us might be so far off the mark that we need to do like the carpenter at the beginning of this article—Humble ourselves and start over.

Husbands are pulling their unwilling wives into the world, wives are pushing their husbands into the world, and children are dragging their parents into the world. And unfortunately, since the modern church has thrown off all forms of discipline and structure, everyone can stay in the church and pollute it with their worldly ideas (at least as long as you smile and say you love Jesus.) Remember the Scriptures: If ye love me, keep my commandments –John 14:15. And, He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him –1 John 2:4.

Here are some areas of drift in the church.

Brotherly love

By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another –John 13:35.

People have visited our church and asked if we practice the holy kiss. I reply that we do; however, understanding the need to love one another comes first. Many churches are doing away with the holy kiss, which is clearly instructed in the Word. And it seems appropriate because they have stopped loving one another. I don’t believe we understand the importance of this topic—having love one for another. When our love causes us to suffer for one another, the world sees it. Often, the reason a brotherhood stops loving each other is because they are not in the fight “together” anymore. They have become independent.

Some of the greatest acts of showing love for one another have happened on the battlefield. Men have jumped on grenades, and they have jumped in front of bullets to save their comrades. Because they have fought together, they look out for each other. What if a soldier marching out to battle would notice a fellow soldier’s ammunition clip fall from his gun? What would he do? Would he remain quiet because his comrade might get mad? Or would he remain quiet because he knew that he had his own problems? No. He would help his brother. If ungodly men on the battlefield can practice this, why can’t God’s people do so in the church? Before I was converted, I was in the military. I chose to suffer for my country. Now that I’m a Christian, I now choose to suffer for my Lord.

Dress

This is the most obvious, but also the most overlooked. The worldly church says, “It’s the heart that counts, so how we appear on the outside doesn’t matter”. Are the Anabaptists falling for this? The world used to dress modestly, but television and Hollywood began to promote a focus on the human body. Surely the church wouldn’t follow Hollywood. But what is the difference—a woman of the world who is obviously dressed immodestly, or a woman of the church dressed with a cape dress that is form-fitting, and with a little covering hanging skimpily on the back of her head? There is little difference, except the one claims to be a Christian and the other one doesn’t. Dear ones, the world is laughing at us.

So how does it all start? Subtly. First remove a pleat here or a gather there, then start using a little less material, finally, start buying brighter bolder colors. The men untuck the shirt, switch to jeans, then skinny jeans, undo a few buttons, grow out the hair a little. Buy a pair of the “cool” name brand shoes, and a cowboy hat. The devil is no fool. If you drop a frog into boiling water, it will jump out quickly. If you boil the water that contains the frog, he will slowly cook to death. Is it too late for us to jump out? With God all things are possible. Brothers and sisters, it is the heart that counts; and if we desire to look like the world, our heart is worldly and needs to be cleaned—cleaned by the ever so powerful blood of Jesus.

Pleasure

Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter. Ye have condemned and killed the just; and he doth not resist you –James 5:5-6.

And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection –Luke 8:14.

This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away –2 Timothy 3:1-5.

When we are given to pleasure, we separate ourselves from the sufferings we have been called to, therefore separating us from the reward received from suffering.

Remember, when we give in a little on any issue during our generation, our children will go farther with it. When our children enjoy going to church only because of the volleyball game that’s scheduled afterward, it’s not good. When they want to go on a mission trip because of the pleasures of the ocean, it’s not good. I’m not saying those things are bad, but when they become the focal point, we have a serious problem. Do we enjoy doing the things that God enjoys? Do we enjoy hymn sings anymore? Do we enjoy helping the poor? What about visiting the widows? I believe if the fathers have their priorities right, and they truly love doing the things of God even if the flesh suffers, then so will our children, (the next generation) for which WE are responsible. I often tell people that they don’t need to follow Jesus. They can love the world, and the pleasures of this life, but they cannot continue sitting in our church and pretend they are Christians. People might say that’s too harsh, but I believe Jesus said the same thing. I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth –Revelation 3:15-16.

This is not a complete list as there are many other ways that the church is drifting towards the world. My prayer is that, first, we could see the problem, and second, we could deal with it. Remember a little leaven leavens the lump. (1 Corinthians 5)

There is a battle that’s raging; the kingdom of darkness is pressing in. The devil truly knows he has but a short time. Let us make a stand, put down our white flags, and pick up our swords. Let us remove the traitors, the world, and the sin that has come into the church. Let us purify the church and fight the good fight of faith.

How do we stop the drift? How do we leave behind a faithful generation? First, the fathers need to teach their children, and the leaders in the church need to teach them all. The early Anabaptists met as many times as they could, and that was usually out in the weather, in some woods somewhere. Our church here meets five times a week. Meeting on Sundays only, I believe, shows where our priorities are.

And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: – Ephesians 4:11-13.

It seems that God would give us teachers, pastors, evangelists, prophets, and apostles if we would use them.

Let’s make this personal—there could be areas of drift in my life. We need to help each other before we all drift into ruin. Maybe we can maintain, but we also need to be concerned about our children. If we could get together and be honest with ourselves and with one another about what the scriptures clearly teach, then we would be more careful. If we could study God’s Word together, with open hearts and minds, I believe we could strengthen that which remains. I believe if we would fall on our faces before God, He would heal our churches. May God bless us all in a deeper walk with Him.

나는 한 남자가 큰 합판 판자를 반으로 자르려고 애쓰는 것을 보았다. 그는 자르는 동안 몇몇 다른 남자들과 이야기를 나누고 있었고, 선을 곧게 자르는 것에 크게 신경 쓰지 않는 듯했다. 나는 그가 못으로 긁어 표시해 둔 선에서 점점 더 멀어져서 자르는 것을 계속하는 것을 알아차렸다. 몇 인치 정도 벗어난 뒤에 그의 친구 중 한 명이 그것을 지적하려 했지만 그는 못 본 척했다. 그는 대수롭지 않게 옛 손톱을 표시선 쪽으로 살짝 이끌어 보려 했고, 사람들과 계속 이야기하면서 크게 문제 삼지 않으려 했다. 마침내 그가 1피트가 넘게 빗나간 뒤에야 멈췄다. 그는 이제 자신에게 문제가 있음을 알았다. 그가 고칠 수 없는 문제였다.

나는 생각하지 않을 수 없었다. “우리가 그리스도의 신부인 교회로서 이러고 있는가?” 우리는 바른 좁은 길에서 조금 벗어나는 것을 심각하게 여기지 않는다. 우리는 세상적인 것들이 우리 가운데 들어오도록 허용한다. 우리는 말한다. “별일 아니야, 너무 비판적일 필요 없어.” 그러나 오래 기다릴수록 바로잡기 힘들어진다. 처음에는 충격적이지만, 나중에는 그것이 새로운 정상(뉴 노멀)이 된다. 우리가 표류했는지 어떻게 알 수 있는가? 우리가 어디에 있었는지를 생각해 보고, 지금 우리가 어디에 있는지와 비교한 다음, 변화가 성경의 가르침과 어떻게 일치하는지 평가하면 간단해야 한다.

표류에 맞서 싸우는 것은 인기가 없기 때문에 교회 안의 사람들은 그것을 하고 싶어하지 않는다. 세상 쪽으로 표류하는 우리 교회의 일부 사람들은 기분좋은 복음을 완성해 냈다. 그들은 예수님과 얼마나 가까워지고 있는지, 얼마나 복을 받았는지 계속 떠들어대지만 그들의 방향은 분명히 성경의 가르침과 맞지 않는다. 그들은 세상을 향해 가고 있다.

표류를 원하지 않는 다른 이들도 있지만 그들에게도 문제가 있다—돈 사랑, 탐욕, 쾌락에 대한 사랑이다. 아무도 말하지 않는다. 아무도 듣고 싶어하지 않는 것처럼 보이기 때문이다. 흔한 반응은 “맞아, 좋은 건 아니지만 우리가 뭘 할 수 있겠나?” “모든 교회에 문제는 있다.” 혹은 “난 결코 그런 걸 허락하지 않겠지만, 그것에 대해 말할 자격이 내게 있는 것 같지 않다.” “우리 가족은 아니지만, 다른 사람들이 원하면 괜찮다.” 같은 말들이다.

우리는 ‘나’의 시대에 살고 있다. 모든 것이 나에 관한 것이다. 보수적인 아나뱁티스트 사람들도 소셜 미디어, 셀피, 트위터, 페이스북 등으로 얽혀들고 있다. 우리는 자신을 드러내는 방식으로 말하고 행동하고 옷 입는 정도로 자신을 사랑한다—우리는 자신을 홍보한다. 우리는 보기 좋고, 기분 좋고, 잘 사는 것에 대해 이야기한다. 예수를 알리는 것은 어찌 된 일인가? 예수님은 말씀하셨다: For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it –Matthew 16:25.

우리가 어느 방향으로 가는지 알아내는 것이 왜 이리 어려워 보이는가? 만약 우리가 온통 우리 자신에 관한 것이라면, 우리는 예수에 관한 것이 아니다. 만약 우리가 최신 유행과 멋진 차, 트럭, 집에 집착한다면, 우리는 예수에 관한 것이 아니다. 우리는 육체를 기쁘게 하는 것을 마음껏 누리면서도 여전히 우리가 그리스도인이라고 말할 수 없다.

나는 최근에 왜 어떤 목사들이 자녀들을 세상에 잃게 되는지에 대해 질문을 받았다. 대부분의 경우, 나는 많은 아나뱁티스트들이 자녀들을 어둠의 왕국으로 잃어가는 이유가 같다고 믿는다—아버지들이 가정에 대한 경건한 비전을 잃었다. 그들은 능력 없는 삶을 살며 세상이 들어오도록 허용한다. 어쩌면 그들은 텔레비전은 없지만 인터넷은 어째서인가? 이것도 여전히 세상의 영향을 들여오는 통로이다. 또한 아버지는 사업에 더 많은 시간을 쓰고 삶을 즐기는 데 더 많은 시간을 쓰며 하나님의 얼굴을 구하는 데는 덜 시간을 쓴다.

많은 미국인들이 단기 선교를 간다. 많은 경우, 선교를 가는 청년들이 비행기에서 내리자마자 해변이나 다른 쾌락과 휴식을 찾고 싶어하는 것처럼 보인다. 왜일까? 왜냐하면 그들이 집에서 그렇게 배우거나 허용받았기 때문이다—쾌락을 추구하도록. 그들은 육체를 부인하는 법을 배우지 못했고, 부모가 육체를 부인하는 것을 보지 못했다. 우리 중 일부는 너무 많이 빗나가서 이 글 처음에 나온 목수처럼 해야 할지도 모른다—겸손히 자신을 낮추고 다시 시작하라.

남편들은 마지못해 따라오는 아내들을 세상 쪽으로 끌어들이고, 아내들은 남편들을 세상 쪽으로 밀어내고, 자녀들은 부모들을 세상 쪽으로 끌고 간다. 그리고 불행히도 현대 교회가 모든 형태의 훈계와 구조를 벗어던진 이후로, 누구든지 교회에 머물며 세상적인 생각들로 그것을 오염시킬 수 있다(적어도 미소 지으며 예수님을 사랑한다고 말하는 한은). 성경을 기억하라: If ye love me, keep my commandments –John 14:15. And, He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him –1 John 2:4.

다음은 교회가 표류하는 몇몇 영역들이다.

형제자매 사랑

By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another –John 13:35.

사람들이 우리 교회를 방문하여 우리가 거룩한 입맞춤을 실천하느냐고 물어본 적이 있다. 나는 그렇다고 대답하지만, 서로 사랑할 필요를 이해하는 것이 먼저라고 말한다. 많은 교회들이 성경에 분명히 지시된 거룩한 입맞춤을 없애고 있다. 그리고 그럴 만하다—그들이 서로 사랑하는 것을 멈췄기 때문이다. 나는 우리가 이 주제—서로에 대한 사랑의 중요성을 이해하지 못한다고 믿는다. 우리가 서로를 위해 고난받게 하는 사랑을 가질 때, 세상은 그것을 본다. 종종, 형제단이 서로 사랑하기를 멈추는 이유는 그들이 더 이상 ‘함께’ 싸우지 않기 때문이다. 그들은 독립적이 되어 버렸다.

서로 사랑을 보인 가장 위대한 행위들 중 일부는 전장에서 일어났다. 사람들이 수류탄에 몸을 던지고, 전우를 구하기 위해 총알 앞에 뛰어든 일들이 있다. 함께 싸웠기 때문에 그들은 서로를 돌본다. 전투에 나가는 병사가 동료 병사의 탄창이 총에서 떨어지는 것을 본다면 어떻게 하겠는가? 그는 조용히 있을 것인가, 동료가 화낼까봐? 아니면 자신에게도 문제가 있으니 조용히 있을 것인가? 아니다. 그는 형제를 도울 것이다. 전장에서 세속인들이 이것을 실천할 수 있다면, 하나님의 백성들이 교회에서 어찌하지 못할 이유가 있는가? 내가 회심하기 전 나는 군대에 있었다. 나는 나라를 위해 고난을 택했다. 이제 내가 그리스도인이 되었으니, 나는 내 주를 위해 고난을 택한다.

복장

이것은 가장 분명하지만 또한 가장 간과되는 것이다. 세속적 교회는 말한다, “중요한 것은 마음이다, 그러니 겉모습은 상관없다.” 아나뱁티스트들이 이것에 속아 넘어가고 있는가? 세상은 예전에는 단정하게 입었지만 텔레비전과 할리우드가 인간의 몸에 초점을 맞추도록 촉진하기 시작했다. 분명 교회가 할리우도를 따르진 않을 것이다. 그러나 차이가 무엇인가—분명히 노출된 옷을 입은 세상 여인과, 형태가 드러나는 케이프 드레스를 입고 뒤에 걸친 가늘게 걸친 작은 머리 덮개를 한 교회 여인 사이에 무엇이 다른가? 거의 차이가 없다. 단지 한 사람은 자신이 그리스도인이라고 주장하고 다른 사람은 그렇지 않을 뿐이다. 사랑하는 이들아, 세상은 우리를 비웃고 있다.

그렇다면 모든 것은 어떻게 시작되는가? 미묘하게. 먼저 여기 한 주름을 없애고 저기 한 주름을 덜어내고, 그다음 조금 덜한 재료를 사용하기 시작하고, 마침내 더 밝고 눈에 띄는 색을 사기 시작한다. 남자들은 셔츠를 빼어내고 청바지로 바꾸고, 그다음 스키니 진으로, 단추 몇 개를 풀고 머리를 조금 기른다. ‘멋진’ 브랜드 신발 한 켤레와 카우보이 모자를 산다. 마귀는 어리석지 않다. 개구리를 끓는 물에 넣으면, 그것은 빠르게 뛰쳐나온다. 만약 개구리를 담고 있는 물을 끓이면, 그는 천천히 삶아 죽을 것이다. 우리가 뛰쳐나오기에 너무 늦었는가? 하나님께는 모든 것이 가능하다. 형제자매들아, 중요한 것은 마음이다; 우리가 세상처럼 보이길 원한다면 우리의 마음은 세속적이며 정화되어야 한다—예수의 강력한 피로 정결함을 받아야 한다.

쾌락

Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter. Ye have condemned and killed the just; and he doth not resist you –James 5:5-6.

And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection –Luke 8:14.

This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away –2 Timothy 3:1-5.

쾌락에 빠질 때 우리는 우리에게 부르심받은 고난에서 스스로를 떼어 놓게 되고, 따라서 고난에서 오는 상으로부터도 스스로를 분리하게 된다.

기억하라, 우리가 어떤 문제에 대해 이 세대에서 조금이라도 양보하면, 우리 자녀들은 그것을 더 멀리 가져간다. 자녀들이 교회를 즐기는 이유가 뒤에 예정된 배구 경기 때문이라면, 그것은 좋지 않다. 그들이 바다의 쾌락 때문에 선교 여행을 가고 싶어한다면, 그것은 좋지 않다. 나는 그 일들이 나쁘다고 말하는 것이 아니다. 그러나 그것들이 초점이 될 때, 우리는 심각한 문제를 가지고 있다. 우리가 하나님이 기뻐하시는 일을 즐기는가? 우리가 찬송 모임을 여전히 즐기는가? 가난한 사람들을 돕는 것을 즐기는가? 과부들을 방문하는 것은 어떠한가? 나는 아버지들이 우선순위를 올바로 세우고, 육체가 고난을 당하더라도 하나님의 일을 사랑하는 것을 진정으로 즐긴다면, 우리 자녀들(다음 세대)도 그럴 것이라고 믿는다. 우리는 그들에 대해 책임이 있다. 나는 자주 사람들에게 말한다—그들은 예수님을 따를 필요가 없다. 그들은 세상과 이 생의 쾌락을 사랑할 수 있다. 그러나 그들이 계속 우리 교회에 앉아 있으면서 자신들이 그리스도인인 척할 수는 없다. 사람들은 그것이 너무 엄하다고 말할지 모른다. 그러나 나는 예수님이 같은 말을 하셨다고 믿는다. I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth –Revelation 3:15-16.

이것이 전부는 아니다. 교회가 세상으로 표류하는 다른 많은 방식들이 있다. 나의 기도는, 첫째로 우리가 문제를 볼 수 있게 되고, 둘째로 우리가 그것을 처리할 수 있게 되는 것이다. 조금의 누룩이 덩이를 부풀게 하는 것을 기억하라. (1 Corinthians 5)

전쟁이 벌어지고 있다; 어둠의 왕국이 압박해 들어오고 있다. 마귀는 참으로 시간이 얼마 없음을 알고 있다. 우리의 흰 깃발을 내려놓고, 검을 들어 반격하자. 반역자들과 세상과 교회 안으로 들어온 죄를 제거하자. 교회를 정결하게 하고 믿음의 선한 싸움을 싸우자.

어떻게 표류를 멈출 것인가? 어떻게 신실한 세대를 남길 것인가? 먼저, 아버지들이 자녀들을 가르쳐야 하고, 교회의 지도자들이 모두 그들을 가르쳐야 한다. 초기 아나뱁티스트들은 가능한 한 자주 모였고, 보통은 야외 어딘가 숲 속에서 모였다. 우리 교회는 여기서 주당 다섯 번 모인다. 주일에만 모이는 것은 우리의 우선순위가 어디에 있는지를 보여준다고 나는 믿는다.

And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: – Ephesians 4:11-13.

하나님은 우리가 그들을 사용하기만 한다면 교사들과 목사들, 전도자들, 예언자들, 사도들을 우리에게 주실 것처럼 보인다.

이것을 개인적으로 만들자—내 삶에도 표류의 영역이 있을 수 있다. 우리는 모두 파멸로 표류하기 전에 서로를 도와야 한다. 어쩌면 우리는 유지할 수 있겠지만, 우리 자녀들에 대해서도 관심을 가져야 한다. 우리가 함께 모여 성경이 분명히 가르치는 바에 대해 우리 자신과 서로에게 솔직할 수 있다면, 우리는 더 조심할 것이다. 열린 마음과 마음으로 함께 하나님의 말씀을 공부할 수 있다면, 나는 우리에게 남아 있는 것을 강화할 수 있다고 믿는다. 우리가 얼굴을 땅에 대고 하나님 앞에 엎드린다면, 그분은 우리의 교회를 고치실 것이라 나는 믿는다. 하나님께서 우리 모두를 그분과 더 깊은 동행으로 축복하시기를.

This story starts in Switzerland, in the 1500s. A group of Christian believers, desiring to obey Jesus and return to the teachings of the Apostles and the early Church, separated from both the Catholic and Protestant state-run Churches in several Cantons of Switzerland. They were referred to as the Swiss Brethren and were deemed as enemies of the state, by the Catholics and Protestants alike. Their enemies called them “Anabaptists” because they rejected infant baptism. They also refused military service, obeying Christ’s commands to “bless them that persecute you” and “love your enemies”. Many were arrested, imprisoned, tortured mercilessly and finally, many were martyred for not recanting their faith. In the early 1600s, when the authorities could not stop the movement in this manner, they began confiscating the believer’s homes, farms, and belongings, then exiled them from Switzerland.

Europe had just gone through the devastations of the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648). In some places, like the Palatinate (Pfaltzland) in Germany, as many as 70% of the inhabitants had died of either war or disease. Many of the Hoffs (house/barn fort enclosures) were burned out and the fields were left uncultivated for years. In the mid-1600s, the local Prince, Elector Ludwig, invited the exiled Swiss Brethren into the Palatinate to help rebuild the farms because of their reputation as excellent husbandmen and tillers of the soil.

There were three official Churches recognized by the Germans: Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed. Although the Swiss Brethren were needed economically, and their faith was tolerated, their churches were not recognized. There were limits on how many of them could meet together at one time, and many times they were not allowed to purchase the farms that they were improving because they were considered foreigners.

The Swiss-operated farms did indeed prosper in time, partly due to their use of a superior crop rotation system, which helped them feed more dairy cattle, and, in turn, allowed them to produce milk through the winters. Another major improvement was the introduction of the legume, clover. This came from seed which the Dutch Mennonites gifted to them. After about 50 years, the difference the Swiss had made in agriculture was noticeable enough that some frustrated German neighbors accused them of “Ferhexing” (the Pennsylvania Dutch term for witchcraft) the ground (which of course was not true). So, life in the Pfaltzland wasn’t getting better for the Swiss Brethren.

In the year 1708, they experienced a bitterly cold, long winter. So cold that some of their stored root crops froze in the cold cellars. Sometime after this, William Penn and the Quakers heard of the plight of these Swiss Anabaptists. In 1682, William Penn had been granted the colony of Pennsylvania and wanted to conduct what he called the “Holy Experiment”. He envisioned a land where all races and religions could dwell together in peace. He had special interest in those groups persecuted by the European State Churches. As a Quaker, he too had suffered persecution by the state church of England. He welcomed Quakers from England, Huguenots from France, Mennonites from Holland, German Baptist, Schwenkfelders and Pietists from Germany, as well as Swiss Brethren and Jews from wherever they were sojourning and/or suffering.

That is the background for our account of Hans Graeff (Groff) who lived from c.1661-1746. Hans had been converted to the faith of the Swiss Brethren, but his wife, Anna (Bare) Graeff had stayed with the Protestant State Church. When the door opened to pioneer in Pennsylvania, Hans was interested in going, but Anna was not. Possibly they planned to have him get settled in over there and then come back for her. Hans first came to Pennsylvania in 1696. Later, Hans ended up leading a small group of the Swiss Brethren (Hans & Christian Herr, Martin Meylin, Jacob Muller, Martin Kendig, Martin Oberholtzer, Wendell Bowman & the Funks to name a few) to Germantown, about seven miles north of Philadelphia in that day, which was the first permanent settlement of the Anabaptists in the New World. Many of those first settlers were from Holland and Sweden and were part of the Mennonite Church of the Netherlands. The Swiss immigrants spent the winter of 1709 in Germantown—the women doing spinning for the many weavers of Germantown and the men traveling to a new Anabaptist settlement at Skippack, where they were learning many of the skills needed to go to the frontier. It seems that here is where the Swiss Brethren first became known as Mennists or Mennonites.

In 1710, the group moved up to the Conestoga Valley where Hans Groff had previously identified some very rich and well-watered lands, 60 miles west of Germantown and civilization. Life would indeed be difficult. Wolves, bears, panthers, bobcats and other predators abounded. There were also elk, timber bison, and whitetail deer in abundance (which were glad to eat whatever the settlers planted). Huge walnut, hickory, chestnuts, maples, white pines, and oaks, some six feet in diameter and over 100 feet tall, covered much of their new lands (except for some open meadows, left by the native Americans and wetlands). These huge trees would need to be cut down by hand with axes and two-man saws. The closest doctor, apothecary, hardware, or general store was 60 miles away. It would be challenging and dangerous work, but they were free! Free to obey their conscience. Free to practice their religion. Free to own land in this beautiful wilderness. Free to love and witness to their neighbors—the Conestoga tribe and French traders. They received a land patent for 10,000 acres for their families and others that might come later.

Partly due to severe persecution, in 1710, a group of Swiss Brethren moved to the Mannheim area of Germany. Seven years later, in 1717, they made the trip across the Atlantic. There were more than 60 families that came to the Conestoga Valley in the fall of that year, including my ancestors, Hans and Magdalena Hess and their three children (they were eventually blessed with a total of 11). You could say that from then on, the floodgates opened, and masses of Anabaptists fled Europe to “Penn’s Promised Land”. From 1730 and later, as this wilderness became tamed, there were also many Lutheran, Reformed, and Catholic people who came over from Germany to find better financial opportunities, filling this part of Pennsylvania with many German-dialect speakers.

I greatly enjoyed speaking with the noted Lancaster County Anabaptist historian, Amos Hoover, while writing this article. He gave many insights and details, but we both agreed, it is challenging to put together all the facts and details from so long ago. Gleaning from a couple authors’ accounts, the story goes something like this:

Misunderstanding

Sometime, after being in Penn’s woods for a number of years, Hans Groff received word that his wife, Anna (Bare) Groff, back in Europe, had passed away. He was very grieved and mourned, as he didn’t know it and wasn’t there to bury her. In a few years, he married Susanna Kendig. They lived first in the Strasburg area, then built a substantial homestead in the area now called Groffdale. This union was blessed with nine children.

Years later, a woman showed up in the community and introduced herself as Mrs. Hans Groff. She had become an Anabaptist in Europe and had made the perilous trip across the Atlantic to find her husband. According to her, a person with the same name as herself had died, and the word given to Hans was not true about his first wife’s death. Hans was mortified, although he was innocent regarding his second marriage. He had no desire to be a polygamist or to commit adultery. The frontier church leaders held counsel and gave a recommendation—that the younger, pioneer wife with so many young children needed the husband to provide for them. It is said that Hans didn’t feel clear to stay with either of them but did support both of his wives and their children financially. He was noted as a tireless traveler, riding to Philadelphia with furs then back out into the vast frontier with blankets, brass kettles and other trade good for the Native Americans. If you have heard or read this account with different details, so have I. Only eternity will reveal all these details exactly.

Medicine

Hans’s first wife chose to live as a single sister in that church community. Instead of becoming bitter with her husband, her God, and her circumstances, she chose a life of service to her neighbors. She lived in a little house, with a small barn (possibly built by Hans for her) on top of a steep hill overlooking Farmersville, called “Cat’s Back Hill”. The ruins of this early 1700s house and barn were still evident less than 50 years ago. Apparently, she was a midwife, before coming to this country and continued in this profession once she was here. She had a lot of experience with growing herbs and making herbal remedies. She was possibly the closest one to being a doctor for many miles around. From what I can find out, she spent her time being a blessing to the local community with her medical knowledge and wisdom, her homemade herbal medicines, and her midwifery. Many of our Lancaster County forefathers may not have survived the rigorous pioneer life if it had not been for this dear Sister’s servanthood and medical knowledge. Interestingly, years later, one of Hans’s sons from the second wife, David Groff, went away to study medicine. Once his studies were completed, he came back as a doctor and helped his father’s first wife minister to the many settlers in fast growing Lancaster County.

This story provides a glimpse into some of the interesting details surrounding the life of conservative Anabaptists just before and during the establishing of Colonial America. There were difficulties involving freedom of religion and worship in their homelands of Europe, but their travels to, and eventual day-to-day living in, a new, free country was acquainted with challenges as well. One encouragement that we can see in this story was the willingness of these individuals to allow God’s principles to guide them each step of the way.

Esta historia comienza en Suiza, en el siglo XVI. Un grupo de creyentes cristianos, deseando obedecer a Jesús y volver a las enseñanzas de los Apóstoles y de la Iglesia primitiva, se separó tanto de la Iglesia católica como de las Iglesias estatales protestantes en varios cantones de Suiza. Se les llamó los Hermanos Suizos y fueron considerados enemigos del Estado, tanto por católicos como por protestantes. Sus enemigos los llamaron “anabautistas” porque rechazaban el bautismo de niños. También se negaron a prestar servicio militar, obedeciendo los mandatos de Cristo de “bendecid a los que os persiguen” y “amad a vuestros enemigos”. Muchos fueron arrestados, encarcelados, torturados sin piedad y, finalmente, muchos fueron martirizados por no renegar de su fe. A principios del siglo XVII, cuando las autoridades no pudieron detener el movimiento de esa manera, comenzaron a confiscar las casas, granjas y pertenencias de los creyentes y luego los exiliaron de Suiza.

Europa acababa de sufrir las devastaciones de la Guerra de los Treinta Años (1618-1648). En algunos lugares, como el Palatinado (Pfaltzland) en Alemania, hasta el 70% de los habitantes había muerto por la guerra o la enfermedad. Muchas de las Hoffs (recintos de casa/granero fortificados) fueron quemadas y los campos quedaron sin cultivar durante años. a mediados de 1600, el príncipe local, el elector Ludwig, invitó a los Hermanos Suizos exiliados al Palatinado para ayudar a reconstruir las granjas debido a su reputación como excelentes agricultores y labradores de la tierra.

Había tres Iglesias oficiales reconocidas por los alemanes: católica, luterana y reformada. Aunque los Hermanos Suizos eran necesarios económicamente y se toleraba su fe, sus iglesias no eran reconocidas. Había límites en cuántos podían reunirse a la vez y muchas veces no se les permitía comprar las granjas que estaban mejorando porque se los consideraba extranjeros.

Las granjas dirigidas por suizos, con el tiempo, prosperaron en parte por su uso de un sistema superior de rotación de cultivos, que les ayudó a alimentar más ganado lechero y, a su vez, les permitió producir leche durante los inviernos. Otra mejora importante fue la introducción de la leguminosa, el trébol. Esta vino de semillas que los menonitas neerlandeses les regalaron. Después de unos 50 años, la diferencia que los suizos habían hecho en la agricultura fue lo suficientemente notable como para que algunos vecinos alemanes frustrados los acusaran de “Ferhexing” (el término en Pennsylvania Dutch para brujería) la tierra (lo cual, por supuesto, no era cierto). Así que la vida en el Pfaltzland no mejoraba para los Hermanos Suizos.

En el año 1708, experimentaron un invierno largo y amargamente frío. Tan frío que algunos de sus cultivos de raíz almacenados se congelaron en los sótanos fríos. Algún tiempo después de esto, William Penn y los cuáqueros escucharon sobre la difícil situación de estos anabautistas suizos. En 1682, a William Penn se le había concedido la colonia de Pensilvania y quería llevar a cabo lo que llamó el “Experimento Santo”. Imaginó una tierra donde todas las razas y religiones pudieran convivir en paz. Tenía un interés especial en aquellos grupos perseguidos por las Iglesias estatales europeas. Como cuáquero, él también había sufrido persecución por la iglesia estatal de Inglaterra. Acogió a cuáqueros de Inglaterra, hugonotes de Francia, menonitas de Holanda, bautistas alemanes, schwenkfeldianos y pietistas de Alemania, así como a Hermanos Suizos y judíos de dondequiera que estuvieran de paso y/o sufriendo.

Ese es el trasfondo de nuestro relato sobre Hans Graeff (Groff), que vivió aproximadamente entre 1661 y 1746. Hans se había convertido a la fe de los Hermanos Suizos, pero su esposa, Anna (Bare) Graeff, se había quedado con la Iglesia estatal protestante. Cuando se abrió la puerta para ser pionero en Pensilvania, Hans estaba interesado en ir, pero Anna no. Posiblemente planearon que él se estableciera allí y luego volviera por ella. Hans vino por primera vez a Pensilvania en 1696. Más tarde, Hans terminó liderando a un pequeño grupo de Hermanos Suizos (Hans & Christian Herr, Martin Meylin, Jacob Muller, Martin Kendig, Martin Oberholtzer, Wendell Bowman & los Funk, por nombrar algunos) a Germantown, a unas siete millas al norte de Filadelfia en aquella época, que fue el primer asentamiento permanente de los anabautistas en el Nuevo Mundo. Muchos de esos primeros colonos eran de Holanda y Suecia y formaban parte de la Iglesia Menonita de los Países Bajos. Los inmigrantes suizos pasaron el invierno de 1709 en Germantown—las mujeres hilando para los muchos tejedores de Germantown y los hombres viajando a un nuevo asentamiento anabautista en Skippack, donde aprendían muchas de las habilidades necesarias para ir a la frontera. Parece que fue allí donde los Hermanos Suizos pasaron a ser conocidos como menonitas o mennistas.

En 1710, el grupo se trasladó al valle de Conestoga, donde Hans Groff había identificado previamente algunas tierras muy ricas y bien abastecidas de agua, a 60 millas al oeste de Germantown y de la civilización. La vida sería realmente difícil. Abundaban lobos, osos, panteras, linces y otros depredadores. También había alces, bisonte de madera y ciervos de cola blanca en abundancia (los cuales estaban más que dispuestos a comer lo que los colonos plantaran). Enormes nogales, nogalinas, castaños, arces, pinos blancos y robles, algunos de seis pies de diámetro y más de 100 pies de altura, cubrían gran parte de sus nuevas tierras (excepto algunos prados abiertos, dejados por los nativos americanos, y humedales). Estos enormes árboles tendrían que ser talados a mano con hachas y sierras de dos hombres. El médico, el boticario, la ferretería o la tienda general más cercana estaban a 60 millas de distancia. Sería un trabajo desafiante y peligroso, pero eran libres. Libres para obedecer su conciencia. Libres para practicar su religión. Libres para poseer tierras en esta hermosa naturaleza salvaje. Libres para amar y testificar ante sus vecinos—la tribu Conestoga y los comerciantes franceses. Recibieron una patente de tierra por 10,000 acres para sus familias y otros que pudieran venir posteriormente.

En parte debido a la persecución severa, en 1710, un grupo de Hermanos Suizos se mudó al área de Mannheim, en Alemania. Siete años más tarde, en 1717, hicieron el viaje a través del Atlántico. Más de 60 familias vinieron al valle de Conestoga en el otoño de ese año, incluidas mis antepasados, Hans y Magdalena Hess y sus tres hijos (eventualmente fueron bendecidos con un total de 11). Puede decirse que a partir de entonces se abrieron las compuertas y masas de anabautistas huyeron de Europa hacia la “Tierra Prometida de Penn”. Desde 1730 en adelante, a medida que esta naturaleza salvaje se fue dominando, también vinieron muchos luteranos, reformados y católicos de Alemania en busca de mejores oportunidades económicas, llenando esta parte de Pensilvania con hablantes de muchos dialectos alemanes.

Disfruté mucho conversar con el conocido historiador anabautista del condado de Lancaster, Amos Hoover, mientras escribía este artículo. Él ofreció muchas ideas y detalles, pero ambos concordamos en que es un desafío reunir todos los hechos y pormenores de épocas tan remotas. Tomando información de un par de autores, la historia sería algo así:

Malentendido

Algún tiempo después de haber estado en los bosques de Penn por varios años, Hans Groff recibió la noticia de que su esposa, Anna (Bare) Groff, allí en Europa, había fallecido. Él quedó muy acongojado y en duelo, ya que no lo sabía y no estuvo allí para enterrarla. Al cabo de unos años, se casó con Susanna Kendig. Vivieron primero en el área de Strasburg y luego construyeron una casa considerable en la zona que hoy se llama Groffdale. Esta unión fue bendecida con nueve hijos.

Años más tarde, una mujer apareció en la comunidad y se presentó como la señora Hans Groff. Ella se había convertido en anabautista en Europa y había hecho el peligroso viaje a través del Atlántico para encontrar a su marido. Según su relato, una persona con el mismo nombre que ella había fallecido, y la información dada a Hans sobre la muerte de su primera esposa no era cierta. Hans quedó mortificado, aunque era inocente respecto a su segundo matrimonio. No tenía deseo de ser polígamo ni de cometer adulterio. Los líderes de la iglesia de la frontera se reunieron en consejo y dieron una recomendación: que la esposa más joven y pionera, con tantos niños pequeños, necesitaba que el esposo la proveyera. Se dice que Hans no se sintió con libertad para quedarse con ninguna de las dos, pero sí sostuvo económica y financieramente a ambas esposas y a sus hijos. Se le conocía como un incansable viajero, montando hasta Filadelfia con pieles y luego regresando a la vasta frontera con mantas, calderos de latón y otros bienes de comercio para los nativos americanos. Si has oído o leído este relato con detalles diferentes, yo también. Solo la eternidad revelará todos esos detalles exactamente.

Medicina

La primera esposa de Hans optó por vivir como hermana soltera en esa comunidad eclesial. En lugar de amargarse con su marido, con su Dios y con sus circunstancias, eligió una vida de servicio a sus vecinos. Vivía en una pequeña casa, con un granero pequeño (posiblemente construido por Hans para ella) en la cima de una empinada colina que domina Farmersville, llamada “Cat’s Back Hill”. Las ruinas de esta casa y granero de principios de 1700 aún eran evidentes hace menos de 50 años. Aparentemente, ella fue comadrona antes de venir a este país y continuó en esa profesión una vez aquí. Tenía mucha experiencia en el cultivo de hierbas y en la elaboración de remedios herbales. Posiblemente era la persona más cercana a ser doctora en muchas millas a la redonda. Según lo que he logrado averiguar, pasó su tiempo siendo una bendición para la comunidad local con su conocimiento médico y sabiduría, sus medicinas herbarias caseras y su partería. Muchos de nuestros antepasados del condado de Lancaster quizá no habrían sobrevivido a la rigurosa vida de pioneros de no haber sido por el servicio y conocimiento médico de esta querida hermana. Curiosamente, años después, uno de los hijos de Hans con la segunda esposa, David Groff, se fue a estudiar medicina. Una vez terminados sus estudios, regresó como médico y ayudó a la primera esposa de su padre a ministrar a los muchos colonos del condado de Lancaster en rápido crecimiento.

Esta historia ofrece una visión de algunos de los detalles interesantes que rodearon la vida de los anabautistas conservadores justo antes y durante el establecimiento de la América colonial. Hubo dificultades relacionadas con la libertad de religión y de culto en sus tierras de origen en Europa, pero sus viajes y la vida cotidiana en un país nuevo y libre también estuvieron llenos de desafíos. Un ánimo alentador que podemos ver en esta historia fue la disposición de estas personas a permitir que los principios de Dios los guiaran en cada paso del camino.

That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling… –Ephesians 1:17-18.

We all have things we pursue in many aspects of our life. We all need to spend time fulfilling our responsibilities at work and at home. As Anabaptist people, we are known to possess a solid work ethic; but that is not all there is to living the Christian life. We may fellowship with likeminded believers from our church or community, but does our Christian life consist of anything more? Does practically living out our Christian life just mean being a member of our church and having personal devotions every day? Are we free to spend most of our day pursuing things that bring worldly gain? Perhaps we think that we need to spend some time as a volunteer or as a missionary in order to have more value in the Kingdom of Heaven.

What is purpose? Do you have purpose? Everyone has things they pursue, whether it is preparing themselves for a certain sport, pursuing a career, or devoting time to a certain hobby. An athlete spends many hours preparing himself for the goal he has set. An individual studying to become a doctor sacrifices many hours of his time with the goal of becoming a physician. What are the things you are pursuing, and do you have a specific goal in mind? More importantly, let’s examine whether the time we are investing in our pursuits now will bring an eternal return.

God has given each of us a responsibility

In Luke 19 is the parable of the nobleman giving his servants talents to invest. Consider the charge he gave his servants in verse 13. He said therefore, A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return. And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come –Luke 19:12-13.

This parable applies to each one of us. Each of us has different responsibilities, from filling our responsibilities at home, to administrative roles in a place of business. While we do not all own equal responsibilities, we have all been given “talents” to use. We all have a place to fill. We should be making the best of the resources we have been given to invest in the Kingdom of Heaven.

Back to my question, “Does living our Christian life just mean being a member of our church and having personal devotions once a day?” If the Lord has given each of us resources to invest, then we need to consider what we are doing with the time we are given every day. Often, we can budget plenty of time pursuing materialistic things such as hunting, sports, vehicles, etc. While all these things can be useful and healthy, do the things we are pursuing have eternal gain? We don’t seem to be afraid to devote hours of our time on our latest project, however it seems we have a hard time finding a place in our schedule for God’s work.

Personal responsibility

It is easy to have the mindset that, unless we are sacrificing our time in some voluntary capacity in a mission-oriented place, then there is not a lot more than can be done for the Kingdom of Heaven. Is that the reality though? Like the servants in the parable, we have each been given resources that we need to “occupy till the Lord returns”. The Lord has placed each of us in a unique place to serve in His kingdom, whether it is at home, on the job, or on the mission field. We have opportunities around us to exercise those gifts and show the love of Christ. The consideration should be whether I am actually seeing those opportunities or missing them because I am not looking for them. The more time we prioritize serving His Kingdom, the more we will see the needs around us. Remember, there are people around us every day that we can influence for God.

Recognizing our opportunities

Some time ago, I had a coworker come to my office and ask me a simple technical question. I was able to answer the question and work resumed as normal. But I had to wonder why he left the shop and came to me. He was within talking distance of multiple other individuals that would have been able to answer his question. Looking back, I realized that I had an opportunity to provide a listening ear and some caring words for this individual. He was facing some serious personal and relational challenges in life, and he needed someone who cared for him. I realized that there was probably a deeper reason he went out of his way to find an answer to his question. Was I the only one there that could have listened and shared with him? Certainly not. It was an opportunity for me. I could have chosen to be annoyed at him because he was taking up my time for something that someone else could have helped him with. But the question is—did I have the humility to recognize that it was an opportunity for me to reach out to him?

Where do I start?

We all have opportunities around us to exercise our talents. Jesus said: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men –Matthew 5:13. Salt always affects its environment no matter what it is used for. If we are compared to salt, then we should be affecting the environment around us all the time. Our Christian life then becomes more than simply going to church or spending some personal time praying and reading the Bible.

Start by asking God to help you see areas where you can serve others in everyday life. You have an opportunity to impact the lives of those around you. It might be your family, coworkers, customers, or people you meet while away from home. The point is, you have the opportunity around you to offer someone help, to encourage them, or to give them a hand. Are you making the best of those opportunities?

Another thing you should do is evaluate your personal life and the time you spend doing other activities. Are there things you are doing which take up your time and that have no benefit in the Kingdom of God? Maybe God has given you a gift that you are hiding instead of using to invest in His Kingdom. Do you spend time praying and seeking God’s will for your life? Do you spend time studying the Word of God? When our personal time with God becomes a higher priority for us, then our time spent pursuing God’s Kingdom will also become a higher priority. Is there sin hindering you from living out your Christian life? Confess it. Repent of it. Then… Go, and sin no more!

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God –Hebrews 12:1-2.

In the beginning of the article, I asked what you are pursuing. Does your life show that fulfilling God’s will is your highest priority, or is there something else that takes that spot? Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost –Romans 15:13. There are people around us that do not have the hope of a better, future life to strive for that we do. It is up to us to share that with others. Ask God for His Spirit to guide you and show you your opportunities. You cannot sit back and wait for the opportunities to come to you; you need to go find them. Go light your world!

That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling… –Ephesians 1:17-18.

हम सभी के जीवन के कई पहलू हैं जिनके पीछे हम चलते रहते हैं। हमें अपने कार्यस्थल और घर पर अपनी जिम्मेदारियों को पूरा करने के लिए समय बिताना पड़ता है। अनाबैप्टिस्ट लोगों के रूप में, हम एक मज़बूत कार्य नीति रखने के लिए जाने जाते हैं; पर ईसाइयत भोगने का पूरा अर्थ केवल इतना नहीं है। हम अपनी कलीसिया या समुदाय के समान विचारधारा वाले विश्वासियों के साथ समुदायिक संबंध रख सकते हैं, पर क्या हमारा ईसाई जीवन इससे अधिक कुछ है? क्या व्यावहारिक रूप से अपना ईसाई जीवन जीना केवल अपनी कलीसिया का सदस्य होना और रोज़ व्यक्तिगत आराधना करना ही है? क्या हम अपना अधिकांश दिन दुनियावी लाभ लाने वाली चीजों के पीछे खर्च करने के लिए स्वतंत्र हैं? शायद हम सोचते हैं कि स्वर्ग के राज्य में अधिक मूल्य पाने के लिए हमें कुछ समय स्वयंसेवक या मिशनरी के रूप में बिताना होगा।

उद्देश्य क्या है? क्या तुम्हारे पास उद्देश्य है? हर किसी के पास ऐसी चीजें होती हैं जिनके पीछे वे चलते हैं—चाहे वह किसी विशेष खेल की तैयारी करना हो, करियर का पीछा करना हो, या किसी शौक को समय देना हो। एक खिलाड़ी अपने निर्धारित लक्ष्य के लिए खुद को तैयार करने में कई घंटे लगाता है। एक व्यक्ति जो डॉक्टर बनने के लिए पढ़ाई कर रहा है, चिकित्सक बनने के लक्ष्य के लिए अपने समय का बड़ा हिस्सा बलिदान करता है। आप किन चीज़ों के पीछे हैं, और क्या आपके मन में कोई विशिष्ट लक्ष्य है? उससे भी महत्वपूर्ण, आइए यह परखें कि क्या हम अभी जिन चीज़ों पर अपना समय निवेश कर रहे हैं, वे हमें शाश्वत प्रतिफल देंगी।

ईश्वर ने हम में प्रत्येक को एक जिम्मेदारी दी है

लूका 19 में कुलीन पुरुष का दृष्टांत है जिसने अपने सेवकों को निवेश के लिए टैलेंट दिए। उसके द्वारा अपने सेवकों को जो आदेश दिया गया, उसे पद 13 में विचार कीजिए। वह कहता है, इसलिए, एक कुलीन पुरुष दूर देश गया कि अपने लिए राज प्राप्त करे, और वापस आए। और उसने अपने दस सेवकों को बुलाकर उन को दस पाउंड दिए, और उन से कहा, "मेरे आने तक यह ग्रहण करो" –लूका 19:12-13।

यह दृष्टांत हम में प्रत्येक पर लागू होता है। हम में से प्रत्येक के अलग-अलग दायित्व हैं—घर पर अपनी जिम्मेदारियाँ निभाने से लेकर किसी व्यापार स्थान पर प्रशासनिक भूमिकाएँ निभाने तक। जबकि हम सभी के समान दायित्व नहीं हैं, हम सभी को उपयोग करने के लिए "टैलेंट" दिए गए हैं। हम में हर किसी का भरने के लिए एक स्थान है। हमें स्वर्ग के राज्य में निवेश करने के लिए दिए गए संसाधनों का सर्वश्रेष्ठ उपयोग करना चाहिए।

मेरे प्रश्न पर वापस आते हैं, “क्या अपना ईसाई जीवन जीना केवल अपनी कलीसिया का सदस्य होना और रोज़ एक बार निजी आराधना करना ही है?” यदि प्रभु ने हम में प्रत्येक को निवेश के लिए संसाधन दिए हैं, तो हमें यह विचार करना चाहिए कि हम हर दिन दिए गए समय के साथ क्या कर रहे हैं। अक्सर, हम भौतिकवादी चीज़ों जैसे शिकार, खेल, वाहनों आदि का पीछा करने में बहुत समय निर्धारित कर लेते हैं। ये सभी चीज़ें उपयोगी और स्वस्थ हो सकती हैं, पर क्या जिन चीज़ों के पीछे हम हैं वे शाश्वत लाभ देती हैं? हमें ऐसा नहीं लगता कि हम अपने नवीनतम प्रोजेक्ट पर घंटों देने में डरते हैं; किन्तु ऐसा लगता है कि हमें अपने कार्यक्रम में ईश्वर के कार्य के लिए स्थान ढूँढने में कठिनाई होती है।

व्यक्तिगत जिम्मेदारी

यह धारणा रखना आसान है कि जब तक हम किसी मिशन-उन्मुख स्थान में किसी स्वैच्छिक योग्यता के लिए अपना समय बलिदान नहीं कर रहे, तब तक स्वर्ग के राज्य के लिए ज्यादा कुछ नहीं किया जा सकता। पर क्या यही वास्तविकता है? दृष्टांत के सेवकों की तरह, हम में प्रत्येक को ऐसे संसाधन दिए गए हैं जिन्हें हमें "प्रभु के लौटने तक ग्रहण" करना चाहिए। प्रभु ने हम में से प्रत्येक को अपनी राज्य में सेवा करने के लिए एक अनूठी जगह दी है—चाहे वह घर पर हो, नौकरी पर हो, या मिशन क्षेत्र में हो। हमारे आसपास ऐसे अवसर हैं जहाँ हम उन उपहारों का अभ्यास कर सकते हैं और मसीह के प्रेम को दिखा सकते हैं। विचार यह होना चाहिए कि क्या मैं वास्तव में उन अवसरों को देख रहा हूँ या उन्हें खो रहा हूँ क्योंकि मैं उन्हें खोज नहीं रहा। जितना अधिक समय हम अपनी प्राथमिकता के रूप में उसके राज्य की सेवा करने को देंगे, उतना ही अधिक हम अपने चारों ओर की आवश्यकताओं को देखेंगे। याद रखें, हमारे चारों ओर रोज लोग हैं जिन्हें हम ईश्वर के लिए प्रभावित कर सकते हैं।

अपने अवसरों को पहचानना

कुछ समय पहले, मेरे एक सहकर्मी मेरे कार्यालय में आए और मुझसे एक साधारण तकनीकी प्रश्न पूछा। मैं प्रश्न का उत्तर दे सका और काम सामान्य रूप से फिर से शुरू हुआ। पर मुझे आश्चर्य हुआ कि वह दूकान छोड़कर मेरे पास क्यों आया। वह कई अन्य व्यक्तियों की बातचीत दूरी के भीतर था जो उसके प्रश्न का उत्तर दे सकते थे। पीछे मुड़कर देखा तो मुझे एहसास हुआ कि मेरे पास इस व्यक्ति के लिए सुनने वाला कान और कुछ सहानुभूतिपूर्ण शब्द देने का अवसर था। वह जीवन में कुछ गंभीर व्यक्तिगत और संबंधजन्य चुनौतियों का सामना कर रहा था, और उसे किसी ऐसे व्यक्ति की जरूरत थी जो उसकी परवाह करता हो। मुझे लगा कि शायद उसके प्रश्न का उत्तर खोजने के लिए उसने खास कर के मेरे पास आने का गहरा कारण था। क्या मैं ही वहाँ अकेला व्यक्ति था जो सुन सकता और उससे बाँट सकता? निश्चित ही नहीं। यह मेरे लिए एक अवसर था। मैं उस पर चिढ़ सकता था क्योंकि वह मेरे समय को ऐसी चीज़ पर ले रहा था जिसकी सहायता कोई और कर सकता था। पर प्रश्न यह है—क्या मेरे पास वह नम्रता थी कि मैं यह पहचान सकूँ कि यह मेरे लिए उसे पहुँचने का एक अवसर था?

मैं कहाँ से शुरू करूँ?

हमारे आसपास हमेशा ऐसे अवसर होते हैं जहाँ हम अपने टैलेंट का प्रयोग कर सकते हैं। यीशु ने कहा: तुम पृथ्वी का नमक हो; पर यदि नमक अपनी खुशबू खो दे तो किस से उसे फिर से नमक किया जाएगा? वह फिर किसी भी काम के लायक नहीं, सिवाय इसके कि उसे बाहर फेंक दिया जाए और लोगों के पाँव तले कुचला जाए—मत्ती 5:13। नमक चाहे किसी भी काम में प्रयुक्त हो, वह अपने वातावरण पर प्रभाव डालता ही है। यदि हम नमक से तुलना किए जा रहे हैं, तो हमें हमेशा अपने चारों ओर के वातावरण को प्रभावित करना चाहिए। तब हमारा ईसाई जीवन केवल कलीसिया जाना या व्यक्तिगत रूप से प्रार्थना व वचन पढ़ने से अधिक हो जाता है।

शुरू करें ईश्वर से प्रार्थना करके कि वह आपको उन क्षेत्रों को देखने में मदद करे जहाँ आप रोज़मर्रा के जीवन में दूसरों की सेवा कर सकते हैं। आपके पास अपने आसपास के लोगों के जीवन पर प्रभाव डालने का अवसर है। वह आपके परिवार, सहकर्मी, ग्राहक, या घर से दूर यात्रा करते समय मिलने वाले लोग हो सकते हैं। मुद्दा यह है कि आपके आस-पास ऐसे अवसर हैं जहाँ आप किसी को मदद दे सकते हैं, उन्हें प्रोत्साहित कर सकते हैं, या उनका हाथ थाम सकते हैं। क्या आप उन अवसरों का सर्वोत्कृष्ट उपयोग कर रहे हैं?

एक और बात जो आपको करनी चाहिए वह है अपने व्यक्तिगत जीवन और अन्य गतिविधियों में बिताए गए समय का मूल्यांकन करना। क्या ऐसी चीज़ें हैं जिनमें आप समय लगा रहे हैं पर जिनका परमेश्वर के राज्य में कोई लाभ नहीं है? शायद परमेश्वर ने आपको कोई उपहार दिया है जिसे आप छुपा रहे हैं बजाए इसके कि उसे उसके राज्य में निवेश करें। क्या आप प्रार्थना में समय बिताते हैं और अपने जीवन के लिए परमेश्वर की इच्छा खोजते हैं? क्या आप परमेश्वर के वचन का अध्ययन करते हैं? जब हमारा परमेश्वर के साथ व्यक्तिगत समय हमारी अधिक प्राथमिकता बन जाता है, तब परमेश्वर के राज्य की सेवा में बिताया गया समय भी अधिक प्राथमिकता बन जाएगा। क्या कोई पाप आपको अपने ईसाई जीवन को जीने से रोक रहा है? उसे स्वीकार करें। उससे पश्चाताप करें। फिर... जाओ, और पुनः पाप न करो!

इसलिए जब हम इतने बड़े सबूतियों के मेघ से चारों ओर घिरे हुए हैं, तो हर बोझ और उस पाप को त्याग दें जो हमें इतनी आसानी से घेरे रखता है, और उस दौड़ को धैर्यपूर्वक चलें जो हमारे समक्ष रखी गई है, हमारी दृष्टि यीशु पर लगाकर जो हमारे विश्वास का आरम्भकर और सिद्धकर्ता है; जिसने उसके सामने रखे गए आनन्द के लिए क्रूस को सहन किया, लज्जा का तिरस्कार करते हुए, और परमेश्वर के सिंहासन के दाहिने भाग पर बैठ गया है—इब्रानियों 12:1-2।

लेख की शुरुआत में, मैंने पूछा कि आप किसके पीछे हैं। क्या आपका जीवन दिखाता है कि परमेश्वर की इच्छा को पूरा करना आपकी सबसे ऊँची प्राथमिकता है, या वहाँ कोई और चीज़ है जो वह स्थान ले रही है? अब आशा के परमेश्वर आप को सब आनन्द और शान्ति से विश्वास में भर दे, ताकि आप आशा में भरपूर हों, पवित्र आत्मा की शक्ति से—रोमियों 15:13। हमारे आस-पास ऐसे लोग हैं जिनके पास हमारे जैसा एक बेहतर, भविष्य जीवन की आशा नहीं है। यह हमारे ऊपर है कि हम इसे दूसरों के साथ बाँटें। परमेश्वर से प्रार्थना करें कि उसकी आत्मा आपको मार्गदर्शन करे और आपके अवसर दिखाए। आप पीछे बैठकर अवसरों के आपके पास आने का इंतज़ार नहीं कर सकते; आपको उन्हें खोजने के लिए जाना होगा। जाइए और अपनी दुनिया को प्रकाश दीजिए!

Freedom, or bondage—which will it be?
Or are they the same; can someone see?

People love things that money can buy,
They trade their lives, with no reason why.

The bills pile up for comforts and ease;
“What about our wives, or children to please?”

We spend all our days chasing the dollar.
The devil smiles as he tightens our collar.

We need time for God, and our families too.
Maybe less time at work could surely do.

Do we have time for that still small voice?
Or does our money talk, and give us no choice?

We all know the Bible—no work, no eat.
But money will bind us until death we meet.

The more we have, the more we need;
The love of money starts with a seed.

Lying to yourself is a foolish thing—
“Freedom, or bondage?” is the question I bring.

¿O son lo mismo; puede alguien verlo?

This story starts in Switzerland, in the 1500s. A group of Christian believers, desiring to obey Jesus and return to the teachings of the Apostles and the early Church, separated from both the Catholic and Protestant state-run Churches in several Cantons of Switzerland. They were referred to as the Swiss Brethren and were deemed as enemies of the state, by the Catholics and Protestants alike. Their enemies called them “Anabaptists” because they rejected infant baptism. They also refused military service, obeying Christ’s commands to “bless them that persecute you” and “love your enemies”. Many were arrested, imprisoned, tortured mercilessly and finally, many were martyred for not recanting their faith. In the early 1600s, when the authorities could not stop the movement in this manner, they began confiscating the believer’s homes, farms, and belongings, then exiled them from Switzerland.

Europe had just gone through the devastations of the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648). In some places, like the Palatinate (Pfaltzland) in Germany, as many as 70% of the inhabitants had died of either war or disease. Many of the Hoffs (house/barn fort enclosures) were burned out and the fields were left uncultivated for years. In the mid-1600s, the local Prince, Elector Ludwig, invited the exiled Swiss Brethren into the Palatinate to help rebuild the farms because of their reputation as excellent husbandmen and tillers of the soil.

There were three official Churches recognized by the Germans: Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed. Although the Swiss Brethren were needed economically, and their faith was tolerated, their churches were not recognized. There were limits on how many of them could meet together at one time, and many times they were not allowed to purchase the farms that they were improving because they were considered foreigners.

The Swiss-operated farms did indeed prosper in time, partly due to their use of a superior crop rotation system, which helped them feed more dairy cattle, and, in turn, allowed them to produce milk through the winters. Another major improvement was the introduction of the legume, clover. This came from seed which the Dutch Mennonites gifted to them. After about 50 years, the difference the Swiss had made in agriculture was noticeable enough that some frustrated German neighbors accused them of “Ferhexing” (the Pennsylvania Dutch term for witchcraft) the ground (which of course was not true). So, life in the Pfaltzland wasn’t getting better for the Swiss Brethren.

In the year 1708, they experienced a bitterly cold, long winter. So cold that some of their stored root crops froze in the cold cellars. Sometime after this, William Penn and the Quakers heard of the plight of these Swiss Anabaptists. In 1682, William Penn had been granted the colony of Pennsylvania and wanted to conduct what he called the “Holy Experiment”. He envisioned a land where all races and religions could dwell together in peace. He had special interest in those groups persecuted by the European State Churches. As a Quaker, he too had suffered persecution by the state church of England. He welcomed Quakers from England, Huguenots from France, Mennonites from Holland, German Baptist, Schwenkfelders and Pietists from Germany, as well as Swiss Brethren and Jews from wherever they were sojourning and/or suffering.

That is the background for our account of Hans Graeff (Groff) who lived from c.1661-1746. Hans had been converted to the faith of the Swiss Brethren, but his wife, Anna (Bare) Graeff had stayed with the Protestant State Church. When the door opened to pioneer in Pennsylvania, Hans was interested in going, but Anna was not. Possibly they planned to have him get settled in over there and then come back for her. Hans first came to Pennsylvania in 1696. Later, Hans ended up leading a small group of the Swiss Brethren (Hans & Christian Herr, Martin Meylin, Jacob Muller, Martin Kendig, Martin Oberholtzer, Wendell Bowman & the Funks to name a few) to Germantown, about seven miles north of Philadelphia in that day, which was the first permanent settlement of the Anabaptists in the New World. Many of those first settlers were from Holland and Sweden and were part of the Mennonite Church of the Netherlands. The Swiss immigrants spent the winter of 1709 in Germantown—the women doing spinning for the many weavers of Germantown and the men traveling to a new Anabaptist settlement at Skippack, where they were learning many of the skills needed to go to the frontier. It seems that here is where the Swiss Brethren first became known as Mennists or Mennonites.

In 1710, the group moved up to the Conestoga Valley where Hans Groff had previously identified some very rich and well-watered lands, 60 miles west of Germantown and civilization. Life would indeed be difficult. Wolves, bears, panthers, bobcats and other predators abounded. There were also elk, timber bison, and whitetail deer in abundance (which were glad to eat whatever the settlers planted). Huge walnut, hickory, chestnuts, maples, white pines, and oaks, some six feet in diameter and over 100 feet tall, covered much of their new lands (except for some open meadows, left by the native Americans and wetlands). These huge trees would need to be cut down by hand with axes and two-man saws. The closest doctor, apothecary, hardware, or general store was 60 miles away. It would be challenging and dangerous work, but they were free! Free to obey their conscience. Free to practice their religion. Free to own land in this beautiful wilderness. Free to love and witness to their neighbors—the Conestoga tribe and French traders. They received a land patent for 10,000 acres for their families and others that might come later.

Partly due to severe persecution, in 1710, a group of Swiss Brethren moved to the Mannheim area of Germany. Seven years later, in 1717, they made the trip across the Atlantic. There were more than 60 families that came to the Conestoga Valley in the fall of that year, including my ancestors, Hans and Magdalena Hess and their three children (they were eventually blessed with a total of 11). You could say that from then on, the floodgates opened, and masses of Anabaptists fled Europe to “Penn’s Promised Land”. From 1730 and later, as this wilderness became tamed, there were also many Lutheran, Reformed, and Catholic people who came over from Germany to find better financial opportunities, filling this part of Pennsylvania with many German-dialect speakers.

I greatly enjoyed speaking with the noted Lancaster County Anabaptist historian, Amos Hoover, while writing this article. He gave many insights and details, but we both agreed, it is challenging to put together all the facts and details from so long ago. Gleaning from a couple authors’ accounts, the story goes something like this:

Misunderstanding

Sometime, after being in Penn’s woods for a number of years, Hans Groff received word that his wife, Anna (Bare) Groff, back in Europe, had passed away. He was very grieved and mourned, as he didn’t know it and wasn’t there to bury her. In a few years, he married Susanna Kendig. They lived first in the Strasburg area, then built a substantial homestead in the area now called Groffdale. This union was blessed with nine children.

Years later, a woman showed up in the community and introduced herself as Mrs. Hans Groff. She had become an Anabaptist in Europe and had made the perilous trip across the Atlantic to find her husband. According to her, a person with the same name as herself had died, and the word given to Hans was not true about his first wife’s death. Hans was mortified, although he was innocent regarding his second marriage. He had no desire to be a polygamist or to commit adultery. The frontier church leaders held counsel and gave a recommendation—that the younger, pioneer wife with so many young children needed the husband to provide for them. It is said that Hans didn’t feel clear to stay with either of them but did support both of his wives and their children financially. He was noted as a tireless traveler, riding to Philadelphia with furs then back out into the vast frontier with blankets, brass kettles and other trade good for the Native Americans. If you have heard or read this account with different details, so have I. Only eternity will reveal all these details exactly.

Medicine

Hans’s first wife chose to live as a single sister in that church community. Instead of becoming bitter with her husband, her God, and her circumstances, she chose a life of service to her neighbors. She lived in a little house, with a small barn (possibly built by Hans for her) on top of a steep hill overlooking Farmersville, called “Cat’s Back Hill”. The ruins of this early 1700s house and barn were still evident less than 50 years ago. Apparently, she was a midwife, before coming to this country and continued in this profession once she was here. She had a lot of experience with growing herbs and making herbal remedies. She was possibly the closest one to being a doctor for many miles around. From what I can find out, she spent her time being a blessing to the local community with her medical knowledge and wisdom, her homemade herbal medicines, and her midwifery. Many of our Lancaster County forefathers may not have survived the rigorous pioneer life if it had not been for this dear Sister’s servanthood and medical knowledge. Interestingly, years later, one of Hans’s sons from the second wife, David Groff, went away to study medicine. Once his studies were completed, he came back as a doctor and helped his father’s first wife minister to the many settlers in fast growing Lancaster County.

This story provides a glimpse into some of the interesting details surrounding the life of conservative Anabaptists just before and during the establishing of Colonial America. There were difficulties involving freedom of religion and worship in their homelands of Europe, but their travels to, and eventual day-to-day living in, a new, free country was acquainted with challenges as well. One encouragement that we can see in this story was the willingness of these individuals to allow God’s principles to guide them each step of the way.

Denne historien begynner i Sveits på 1500-tallet. En gruppe kristne troende, som ønsket å adlyde Jesus og vende tilbake til apostlenes og den tidlige kirkes lære, skilte seg fra både den katolske og den protestantiske statskirken i flere kantoner i Sveits. De ble omtalt som de sveitsiske brødre og ble av både katolikker og protestanter ansett som statens fiender. Deres fiender kalte dem «anabaptister» fordi de avviste barnedåp. De nektet også militærtjeneste, og adlød Kristi befalinger om å «velsigne dem som forfølger dere» og «elsk deres fiender». Mange ble arrestert, fengslet, torturert nådeløst og til sist martyret fordi de ikke ville fornekte sin tro. På tidlig 1600-tall, da myndighetene ikke lenger kunne stanse bevegelsen på denne måten, begynte de å konfiskere troendes hjem, gårder og eiendeler, og deretter forviste dem fra Sveits.

Europa hadde nettopp gjennomlevd ødeleggelsene fra trettiårskrigen (1618–1648). På noen steder, som i Pfalz (Pfaltzland) i Tyskland, var så mye som 70 % av innbyggerne døde av enten krig eller sykdom. Mange av de såkalte Hoffs (hus/loft befeste lser) var brent ut, og åkrene ble liggende urørte i flere år. På midten av 1600-tallet inviterte den lokale fyrsten, kurfyrste Ludwig, de eksilerte sveitsiske brødrene til Pfalz for å hjelpe til med å bygge opp gårdene igjen, på grunn av deres rykte som dyktige jordbrukere og jorddyrkere.

Det var tre offisielle kirker anerkjent av tyskerne: katolsk, luthersk og reformert. Selv om de sveitsiske brødrene var økonomisk nyttige og deres tro ble tolerert, ble deres menigheter ikke anerkjent. Det var begrensninger på hvor mange av dem som kunne møtes samtidig, og ofte ble de nektet å kjøpe gårdene de forbedret fordi de ble regnet som fremmede.

De sveitsisk-drevne gårdene blomstret etter hvert, delvis på grunn av deres bruk av et overlegent vekstskifte, som hjalp dem å føde flere melkekyr, og som igjen gjorde dem i stand til å produsere melk gjennom vintrene. En annen stor forbedring var innføringen av belgveksten kløver. Dette kom fra frø som de nederlandske mennonittene ga dem. Etter omtrent 50 år var forskjellen de sveitsiske innvandrerne hadde gjort i jordbruket synlig nok til at noen frustrerte tyske naboer anklaget dem for å «ferhexing» (Pennsylvania‑dutch uttrykk for heksekunst) jorden (hvilket selvsagt ikke var sant). Så livet i Pfaltzland ble ikke enklere for de sveitsiske brødrene.

I året 1708 opplevde de en bitterlig kald, lang vinter. Så kald at noen av deres lagrede rotgrønnsaker frøs i de kalde kjellerne. Noen år etter dette fikk William Penn og kvakerne høre om de sveitsiske anabaptistenes nød. I 1682 hadde William Penn fått tildelt kolonien Pennsylvania og ønsket å gjennomføre det han kalte «Det hellige eksperiment». Han så for seg et land hvor alle raser og religioner kunne bo sammen i fred. Han hadde spesiell interesse for de gruppene som ble forfulgt av de europeiske statskirkene. Som kvaker hadde han også lidd forfølgelse fra Englands statskirke. Han ønsket velkommen kvakere fra England, hugenotter fra Frankrike, mennonitter fra Nederland, tyske baptister, schwenkfeldere og pietister fra Tyskland, samt sveitsiske brødre og jøder fra hvor enn de oppholdt seg og/eller led.

Det er bakgrunnen for vår beretning om Hans Graeff (Groff) som levde ca. 1661–1746. Hans hadde blitt omvendt til troen til de sveitsiske brødrene, men hans kone, Anna (Bare) Graeff, hadde blitt værende i den protestantiske statskirken. Da døren åpnet seg for å pionere i Pennsylvania, var Hans interessert i å dra, men Anna var det ikke. Muligens planla de at han skulle slå seg ned der borte først og så komme tilbake for henne. Hans kom først til Pennsylvania i 1696. Senere endte Hans opp med å lede en liten gruppe av de sveitsiske brødrene (Hans & Christian Herr, Martin Meylin, Jacob Muller, Martin Kendig, Martin Oberholtzer, Wendell Bowman & Funk-familiene for å nevne noen) til Germantown, omkring sju mil nord for Philadelphia på den tiden, som var den første permanente bosetningen av anabaptistene i den nye verden. Mange av de første nybyggerne var fra Holland og Sverige og tilhørte mennonittkirken i Nederland. De sveitsiske immigrantene tilbrakte vinteren 1709 i Germantown—kvinnene spant for de mange veverne i Germantown, og mennene reiste til en ny anabaptistbosetning ved Skippack, hvor de lærte mange av ferdighetene som trengtes for å dra til grensen. Det ser ut til at det var her de sveitsiske brødrene først ble kjent som mennister eller mennonitter.

I 1710 flyttet gruppen opp til Conestoga‑dalen hvor Hans Groff tidligere hadde identifisert noen meget rike og godt vannede landområder, 60 mil vest for Germantown og sivilisasjonen. Livet ville virkelig bli vanskelig. Ulver, bjørner, pantere, gauper og andre rovdyr var tallrike. Det fantes også elg, skogbison og hvithalehjort i overflod (som gjerne spiste det nybyggerne plantet). Store valnøtt-, hickory-, kastanje-, lønnetrær, hvitfuruer og eiketrær, noen seks fot i diameter og over 100 fot høye, dekket mye av deres nye land (bortsett fra noen åpne enger etter urbefolkningen og våtmarker). Disse enorme trærne måtte felles for hånd med økser og tosmanns sager. Den nærmeste lege, apotek, jernvare- eller kolonialbutikk var 60 mil unna. Det ville være krevende og farlig arbeid, men de var frie! Frie til å følge sin samvittighet. Frie til å praktisere sin religion. Frie til å eie jord i denne vakre villmarken. Frie til å elske og vitne for sine naboer—Conestoga‑stammen og franske handelsmenn. De mottok et jordbrev på 10 000 mål for sine familier og andre som kanskje kom senere.

Dels på grunn av hard forfølgelse flyttet en gruppe sveitsiske brødre i 1710 til Mannheim‑området i Tyskland. Syv år senere, i 1717, foretok de reisen over Atlanteren. Det var mer enn 60 familier som kom til Conestoga‑dalen høsten det året, inkludert mine forfedre, Hans og Magdalena Hess og deres tre barn (de ble til slutt velsignet med totalt 11). Man kan si at derfra åpnet slusene seg, og mengder av anabaptister flyktet fra Europa til «Penns lovede land». Fra 1730 og utover, etter hvert som denne villmarken ble temmet, kom det også mange lutheranere, reformerte og katolikker fra Tyskland for å finne bedre økonomiske muligheter, og fylte denne delen av Pennsylvania med mange tysktalende dialekter.

Jeg satte stor pris på å snakke med den kjente Anabaptist‑historikeren fra Lancaster County, Amos Hoover, mens jeg skrev denne artikkelen. Han gav mange innblikk og detaljer, men vi var begge enige om at det er utfordrende å sette sammen alle fakta og detaljer fra så lenge siden. Ut fra et par forfatteres beretninger går historien omtrent slik:

Misforståelse

Noen år etter å ha vært i Penns skoger et antall år, fikk Hans Groff beskjed om at hans kone, Anna (Bare) Groff, hjemme i Europa, hadde gått bort. Han ble dypt bedrøvet og sørget, siden han ikke visste det og ikke var der for å begrave henne. Etter noen år giftet han seg med Susanna Kendig. De bodde først i Strasburg‑området, og bygde senere et betydelig hjemsted i området som nå kalles Groffdale. Dette ekteskapet ble velsignet med ni barn.

År senere dukket en kvinne opp i menigheten og introduserte seg som fru Hans Groff. Hun hadde blitt anabaptist i Europa og hadde gjort den farefulle reisen over Atlanteren for å finne sin mann. Ifølge henne var en person med samme navn som henne død, og ordet som var gitt til Hans om hans første kones død var ikke sant. Hans ble forferdet, selv om han var uskyldig i forbindelse med sitt andre ekteskap. Han hadde ingen ønsker om å være polygamist eller å begå ekteskapsbrudd. Grensekantens kirkeledere rådslåtte og kom med en anbefaling—den yngre pionerkonen med så mange små barn trengte at mannen forsørget dem. Det sies at Hans ikke følte seg klar for å bli hos noen av dem, men han støttet begge sine koner og deres barn økonomisk. Han var kjent som en utrøttelig reisende, ridende til Philadelphia med pelsverk og så tilbake ut til den vide grensen med tepper, kobberkjele og andre byttevarer for de innfødte. Hvis du har hørt eller lest denne beretningen med andre detaljer, så har jeg det også. Bare evigheten vil avsløre alle disse detaljene nøyaktig.

Medisin

Hans’ første kone valgte å leve som en ugift søster i den kirkesamfunnet. I stedet for å bli bitter mot sin mann, sin Gud og sine omstendigheter, valgte hun et liv i tjeneste for sine naboer. Hun bodde i et lite hus, med en liten låve (muligens bygget av Hans for henne) på toppen av en bratt høyde med utsikt over Farmersville, kalt «Cat’s Back Hill». Ruinene av dette tidlige 1700‑talls huset og låven var fortsatt synlige for mindre enn 50 år siden. Tilsynelatende var hun jordmor før hun kom til dette landet, og fortsatte i dette yrket etter at hun kom hit. Hun hadde mye erfaring med å dyrke urter og lage urtepreparater. Hun var muligens den nærmeste man hadde til en lege i mange mils omkrets. Så vidt jeg kan finne ut, brukte hun sin tid på å være en velsignelse for lokalsamfunnet med sin medisinske kunnskap og visdom, sine hjemmelagde urtelegemidler og sitt jordmoryrke. Mange av våre forfedre i Lancaster County ville kanskje ikke ha overlevd det harde pionerlivet hvis det ikke hadde vært for denne kjære søsterens tjeneste og medisinske kunnskap. Interessant nok dro en av Hans’ sønner fra den andre kona, David Groff, senere bort for å studere medisin. Da studiene var fullført kom han tilbake som lege og hjalp sin fars første kone med å tjene de mange nybyggerne i det raskt voksende Lancaster County.

Denne historien gir et glimt av noen av de interessante detaljene som omga livet til konservative anabaptister rett før og under etableringen av kolonial‑America. Det var vanskeligheter knyttet til religionsfrihet og gudstjeneste i deres hjemland i Europa, men deres reiser til, og det daglige livet i, et nytt fritt land var også forbundet med utfordringer. En oppmuntring vi kan se i denne beretningen var villigheten hos disse menneskene til å la Guds prinsipper veilede dem hvert skritt på veien.
